utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-98-29/1-A, the Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. May I first ask Mr. Milosevic if he can hear me and follow the proceedings through the translation. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I can hear you very well and understand and I am able to follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I now call for the appearances. For the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Paul Rogers appearing for the Prosecution, together with my learned friends Ms. Barbara Goy, Mr. Francois Boudreault, and Mr. Matteo Costi, and our case manager today, Ms. Lourdes Galicia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Branislav Tapuskovic, attorney-at-law, and I represent Mr. Dragomir Milosevic; and my assistant is Madam Branislava Isailovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, this is the appeal hearing in the case of the Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic. At the outset, I will briefly summarise the appeals which are pending before the Appeals Chamber and the manner in which we will proceed this morning. Both Mr. Milosevic and the Prosecution have appealed the trial judgement rendered on 12th December, 2007, by Trial Chamber III composed of Judge Robinson, Kesia-Mbe Mindua, and Harhoff. The Trial Chamber found Mr. Milosevic guilty pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute of the crimes of terror, Count 1; murder, Counts 2 and 5; and inhumane acts, Counts 3 and 6. As a consequence of the conviction entered under Count 1, the Trial Chamber dismissed the charges of unlawful attacks against civilians under Counts 4 and 7, as impermissibly cumulative on the ground that the elements of the crime of unlawful attack against civilians are fully encompassed by the crime of terror. The Trial Chamber imposed a single sentence of 33 years of imprisonment. The Trial Chamber, in reaching its verdict and sentence, found that during the indictment period, the SRK under Milosevic's command was responsible for continuously sniping and shelling the area of Sarajevo, resulting in the killing and serious injury of many civilians. It noted that throughout the siege, the civilian population was subjected to conditions of extreme fear and insecurity, which, combined with the inability to leave the city, resulted in deep and irremovable mental scars on that population as a whole. The Trial Chamber concluded that in these circumstances, every incident of sniping and shelling for which the SRK was found responsible was deliberately conducted with the intent to terrorise the civilian population in Sarajevo. It found that these acts also qualified as unlawful attacks against civilians and civilian population under Article 3 of the Tribunal's Statute. Further, the Trial Chamber found that the SRK's military campaign in Sarajevo was a "classical illustration of a large-scale and organised attack, that is, a widespread and systematic attack" constitutive of crimes against humanity. The Trial Chamber further concluded that Milosevic's orders to target civilians in Sarajevo formed part of the continuous strategy of sniping and shelling of civilians commenced under Galic's command. It also found that he planned and ordered those attacks with the intent to spread terror among the population. I will start by recalling Mr. Milosevic's appeal. Mr. Milosevic filed his Notice of Appeal on 11 January 2008 and his Appeal Brief on 14 August 2008. The Prosecution filed its Response Brief on 23 September 2008. Mr. Milosevic's reply was filed on 9 October 2008. Public redacted versions of the confidential briefs have been subsequently filed by both parties. In his appeal, Mr. Milosevic seeks an acquittal of all charges. He sets forth 12 grounds of appeal. In his first ground of appeal, he argues that the Trial Chamber misapplied the law on the crime of terror and the crimes against humanity of murder and inhumane acts, violated the presumption of innocence, and failed to establish beyond reasonable doubt the essential elements of the crimes he was convicted of. In his second and third grounds of appeal, Milosevic further contends that the Trial Chamber violated Rule 89 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence by making findings not supported by evidence on the record and failing to consider the evidence as a whole. In his fourth ground of appeal, Milosevic alleges that the Trial Chamber erroneously set out and applied the law with respect to the civilian status of the trams targeted in sniping incidents, the definition of "siege" and on the issue of his alibi defence. Furthermore, with his sixth to 11th ground of appeal, Milosevic contests the Trial Chamber's factual findings that areas of Sarajevo were civilian zones, that the SRK was behind specific sniper fire or mortar shelling, as well as the findings concerning the possession, use, and origin of aerial bombs. Finally, in his 12th ground of appeal Milosevic challenges the Trial Chamber's findings that he ordered the sniping and shelling of civilians. On the matter of sentencing, addressed in his fifth ground of appeal, Milosevic argues that the Trial Chamber wrongly considered the elements of the crimes as aggravating factors. The Prosecution responds that Milosevic's appeal should be dismissed in its entirety. Let me now turn to the Prosecution's appeal. The Prosecution filed its Notice of Appeal on 31st December 2007 and its Appeal Brief on 30 January 2008. Milosevic responded on 6 August 2008. The Prosecutor replied to Milosevic's Response on 12th August, 2008. The Prosecution raises a single ground of appeal, arguing that the Trial Chamber abused its discretion by imposing a manifestly inadequate sentence. It requests that the original sentence be replaced by a sentence of life imprisonment. In response, Milosevic argues that the facts underlying his convictions were not established beyond reasonable doubt, rendering the sentencing matters moot. In the alternative, he insists that all the relevant mitigating circumstances taken into account by the Trial Chamber should be maintained. During this appeal briefing, the parties may argue the grounds of appeal in the order they consider most suitable for their presentation. However, I would urge the parties not to simply repeat verbatim or summarise extensively what is in the briefs, as the Court is aware of the contents of the briefs and has studied them. I also wish to note that in the addendum to the Scheduling Order of 6 July 2009, the Appeals Chamber has invited the parties to address specific issues during this hearing, issues that do not have to be restated here now. This invitation is made, I want to stress, without prejudice to any matter the parties or the Appeals Chamber will wish to raise and in no way constitutes an expression of an opinion of the Appeals Chambers on the merits of the appeals. I would now like to briefly recall the criteria applicable to errors of fact and law alleged on an appeal. The appeal is not a trial de novo and the appellants must not merely repeat the case from the trial level. Rather, in accordance with Article 25 of the Statute, the appellants must limit their arguments to alleged errors of law which invalidate the decision or alleged errors of fact occasioning a miscarriage of justice. Additionally, it should be recalled that the appellants have an obligation to provide precise references to materials supporting their arguments on appeal. Now, this hearing will proceed according to the addendum to the Scheduling Order issued on 6th July, 2009. The Defence will present its submissions this morning for one hour, 30 minutes. Following a pause, they will continue their submissions for another 30 minutes. Afterwards, the Prosecution will present its response for one hour, and after one hour 30 minutes' pause, continue for one more hour. And accordingly, the hearing will be proceed as scheduled with the adjustments that may be necessary if they occur. It will be most helpful to the Appeals Chamber if the parties could present their submissions in a precise and clear manner. I wish to remind the parties that the Judges may interrupt them at any time to ask questions or the Judges may prefer to ask questions following each party's submission. Let me finally clarify that of course the parties need not use all the time allotted to them if they believe it's not necessary to make full use of it. Having elaborated on the manner in which we will proceed today, I would now like to invite the Defence to present submissions in support of its appeal. Please, Mr. Tapuskovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will now have an opportunity to present certain matters to you in relation to the responsibility of Dragomir Milosevic. In keeping with the order of the Appeals Chamber of the 6th of July, 2009, these oral arguments will be limited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and key arguments of the grounds of appeal will be explained, or rather, predominantly it's the first ground of appeal which largely relates to the other grounds of appeal as well. We will be dealing with these matters until the break and we should like to address the matters that you raised after the break. However, should the Chamber have any questions for us, I should like to focus on the facts upon which law applies, whereas my learned friend would be the one to answer any questions related to legal matters. Let me start at paragraph 7 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber found that the Defence of the accused asserted that the area of Sarajevo could not be characterised as a civilian area and that this was the key argument of the Defence. This is by all means a key issue and it is on the answer to this question that the finding of the responsibility of Dragomir Milosevic under Article 7(1) of the Statute depends. Save for this particular statement on the key argument of the Defence, at paragraph 889, the Trial Chamber also advances its position that the status of the population during the conflict was of crucial importance for the indictment as a whole. That's why at the start of its evaluation of evidence, at paragraph 889, the Chamber first dealt with the status of the population of Sarajevo in the urban areas of the town under the control of the ABiH. This essential, decisive factual dilemma is -- is crucial. The notion of civilian population and the civilian area is a legal notion which is regulated by legal authorities, which the Tribunal regularly applies, and this is something that the Defence dealt with in detail at paragraphs 27 to 32 of the appeals. When the law is applied to the evidence contained in the case record, one can by no means arrive at the findings at which the Trial Chamber arrived on the issue. These conclusions of the Trial Chamber are, in fact, directly opposed to the plethora of evidence adduced. You will, of course, already be aware of that since in the fourth ground of our appeal, fourth subground, we stated that the Trial Chamber completely disregarded certain evidence presented by the Defence. In view of your position expressed in the Halilovic case at paragraph 124, that the fact that a Trial Chamber does not cite relevant evidence provides an indication of the fact that the Trial Chamber did not take the relevant evidence into consideration to begin with. In other words, it disregarded the relevant evidence. I will now be dealing precisely with the evidence that the Trial Chamber did not cite, in other words, did not consider at all and subsequently did not evaluate. Of course it is the understanding of the appellant that it is only by pointing to the disregarded, omitted, specific evidence that he can meet his obligations on the appeal. At paragraphs 1 through 145 of the Appeal Brief, a detailed analysis was presented of the evidence disregarded and omitted and which would have been suitable for drawing reasonable conclusions that the areas of Sarajevo under the ABiH control did not have a civilian status and that the attacks, when launched by the forces of the SRK, were not directed against a civilian population. In our today's submissions we will only be pointing your attention to a number of instances where the Trial Chamber's findings stand in apparent opposition to the evidence in the case file. At paragraph 896 the Trial Chamber found that 40.000 to 45.000 soldiers had not been stationed in densely populated areas. What is not clear is why there would not have been 40.000 to 50.000 soldiers there at all, as found at paragraph 75 of the judgement. In fact, it is stated that many soldiers were deployed in trenches or at positions along the line of confrontation and the footnote to that paragraph refers to the evidence on the ABiH offensive. Many soldiers. How many soldiers are they? That sort of expression "many" doesn't mean anything. It could be 50.000 or let it be 45.000. These are regular units of the ABiH which, according to paragraph 71 of the judgement had 225.000 soldiers. A quarter of the entire ABiH was permanently present in the part of Sarajevo controlled by this army. These were soldiers of the 12th Division stationed in Sarajevo throughout the relevant period of the indictment, and we know full well that the 1st Corps had 78.000 soldiers. The 78.000 soldiers faced 18.000 SRK soldiers. At the time of the relevant period in the indictment there were fewer of them. There were roughly 15.000 of them, because according to the evidence in the case file around 3.000 soldiers had lost their lives by the start of the period relevant to the indictment. Such a large number of regular soldiers of the ABiH who were constantly present in the area of the town that was under their control was an essential factor to be taken into consideration in drawing every particular conclusion in relation to the status of the population in Sarajevo in -- of the parts of Sarajevo under the ABiH control. When it comes to the number of the armed persons intermingled with the civilian population, in the part where the Trial Chamber assesses the evidence concerning the status of the population in Sarajevo under the ABiH control, the Chamber does not even refer to the police forces of the MUP of BiH. Throughout the judgement, it treats them solely as forces charged with maintaining law and order in a strictly civilian environment and not as a force engaging in any sort of support action to military operation in the way this was defined in Article 59, item 3 of the Additional Protocol of Geneva Conventions. At paragraph 190 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber deals with the police forces of the MUP of the BiH. In that paragraph, the Chamber found that the BH police units were not part of the ABiH. The Trial Chamber found that the evidence indicated that the units were under the command of the government and the MUP of the BiH. The Trial Chamber concludes that the evidence did not substantiate a conclusion that the regular police was part and parcel of the forces of the ABiH or that the regular police assisted in the combat operations during ABiH offensives. The Trial Chamber arrives at such a conclusion by stating at paragraph 188 that the strength of the MUP BiH was at around 11.000 or 12.000 members, which, had these police units in fact been engaged in military operations, would have increased significantly the number of armed persons in Sarajevo under the control of the ABiH. And this would have had a bearing on the establishment of the status of the population. Firstly, there exists apparent contradictions in the findings at paragraph 190 and the findings at paragraph 188. Thus, at paragraph 188, cases are referred to where the police forces were used for military actions, particularly for its special units. These are detachments Bosna and Lasta. Even if we disregard this fact, the finding of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 190, that the evidence did not substantiate the -- a conclusion that the regular police assisted in the -- in the combat operations during the ABiH offensive stands in direct contradiction to the evidence adduced, the evidence which the Trial Chamber did not take into consideration at all. I will now be dealing precisely with the evidence indicating that the MUP units were part and parcel of the ABiH and that, as such, they took part in combat operations together with the units of the 1st Corps of the ABiH. I will be now referring you to the Defence evidence that the Trial Chamber completely disregarded in arriving at their findings. D190, D417, D426, and D282. I will now be dealing, because of the restrictions of time, only with one. This is a document of the 12th Division at -- we cannot be calling up the document, but at page 6 of the English version of D190 it is stated: "The forces of the 12th Division with elements of other forces" - and let me not read through everything. The document previously states that they were active in the part of the town under the control of the ABiH, and together with HVO units they refer to the unit Tvrtko, Kralj Tvrtko, so these are the forces that, in coordination with the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were to engage in and what follows next is the precise axis of attack. It is stated: "The command of the 12th Division will organise coordinated action of the 155th Brigade, 102nd Brigade with MUP units and" -- the document again repeats that "the support to be provided by the units of the MUP of the BiH should be precisely defined in this coordinated action." Now, why did I select this document? Because it is obvious that the MUP forces from the Stupsko Brdo, which is an elevation in Sarajevo, acted independently. It is quite clear that in this particular case it was the Ministry of the Interior which had them under their command, whereas in this document the MUP was placed under the direct command of the ABiH; in this other case, the MUP acted independently and was under the command of the MUP leadership. These other documents I referred to also show how the police on a constant basis acted together with the military in the combat operations, starting from June all the way through to the end of the indictment period. Based on the foregoing, it can be concluded that the police forces of the MUP had permanently been engaged in military actions and providing support to military operations. The full strength of both military and police forces which acted together is not -- or was not the subject of deliberations of the Trial Chamber and it was not something that the Trial Chamber took into consideration in arriving at conclusions on the status of the population in Sarajevo. And this is, you will understand, of crucial importance in understanding if this was indeed a civilian area. We will be indicating to you what sort of activity took place there in the indictment period. When it comes to the number of the soldiers of the ABiH which the SRK confronted together with its 15.000 soldiers that it had during the indictment period, we will be indicating something else. At paragraph 897 of the judgement it is stated that there was evidence indicating that during the summer offensive soldiers of other corps of the ABiH provided support to the soldiers of the 1st Corps. We can agree with the finding of the Trial Chamber in the paragraph that there was no evidence indicating that soldiers of the ABiH started arriving en masse to the area of Sarajevo under the control of the ABiH. In paragraph 784 attacks that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina carried out as of May 1995 to the positions of the SRK are referred to. In that paragraph the statement by Major Veljkovic is assessed about the total number of the ABiH soldiers who took part in these attacks because he claimed that in Operation T-95, 61.5 per cent of the total forces of the ABiH took part, namely between 130 to 135.000 soldiers against 15.000 of SRK soldiers at the time time-period covered by the indictment. The Trial Chamber notes that the statement by Major Veljovic about the total ABiH number is not substantiated by other evidence for these operations. That is why I'm going to cite only the numbers of the documents indicating opposite of what is stated in the judgement. These are documents D106, D190, D384, D388, D386, and D390. From Exhibit D190, it can be seen that in the assault actions as of June 1995 onwards, the 1st Corps is joined by the forces of the 3rd, 4th, and the 7th Corps. As it can be seen in the other exhibits that we referred to, it can be seen precisely how many soldiers each of the corps has, and then it can be established that in these joint actions a much larger number of soldiers took part than the cited number of 135.000. These facts about the overall number of the ABiH number of soldiers are of major importance for the actions of the accused at the time of the -- covered by the indictment. The SRK was in a total encirclement at all positions until the end of the conflict, and according to evidence at the time, sustained the bulk of casualties, both in its ranks and also in the civilian area in their area of responsibility. As for the military activities of those 45.000 soldiers, in paragraph 896 the regular execution of military activities is referred to, and the Trial Chamber sees the only activity of those soldiers as them visiting their homes from the line of separation and concludes that the total effect of their movement did not change the civilian status of those urban areas. The conclusion that this movement of 45.000 soldiers - and I indicated in the documents that together with the police forces this number actually amounted to 60.000 - so the movement of these soldiers from the trenches to their homes had the only objective, as referred to by the Trial Chamber, as actually completely opposite to the evidence on the offensive of the ABiH in the entire series of ABiH documents, and these are not actually referred to at all in the footnotes relating to paragraph 896. In paragraph 898 it is concluded that it is clear that within the line of conflict there were military targets. For example, and this is stated in the judgement, on a military map of the BiH army about 30 command posts of army BiH units were shown which were deployed throughout the entire area within the area of conflict. In the footnote for this conclusion, the Trial Chamber refers to one single piece of evidence, and that is map P194. Evaluating that single exhibit, it is concluded that those command posts, as military targets, were not of a sufficient number so that the entire urban area within the area of conflict would be considered as losing their civilian status. Of course you're going to look at this map. Not only did the Trial Chamber in establishing the existence of military facilities in the territory of Sarajevo under the control of the B&H army use only that single exhibit and disregarded a multitude of other exhibits, but it only records the command posts therein. The map shows much more. The command posts were deployed throughout the territory of Sarajevo under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and always it was in the heart of the area of responsibility of specific brigades of the 12th Division which was deployed in that area. And based on that, it can be easily seen that the 102nd, 155th, 101st, 115th, 152nd, 105th, 111th, and the 112th Brigade of the 12th Division, as well as the 104th Brigade of the 14th Division of the 1st Corps of the B&H army were deployed throughout the entire territory of the town of Sarajevo under the control of the B&H army during the time-period covered by the indictment. The map also indicates not only what I referred to but also that the cited brigades are really covering the entire territory of that part of town. Also visible on the map are the positions of battalions of all the cited brigades, some of which have as many as four battalions each. It's true, the positions of lower-ranking units are not recorded which have fewer fighters, but we know that they're there from other exhibits. What is more, the map also indicates the positions of heavy weaponry throughout the entire area of the area of responsibility of these brigades. For example, it indicates the positions of mortars of the 101st Division in the very town centre. We asked -- we would ask the Appeals Chamber to look at the contents of paragraph 81 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber there states that the 1st Corps of the B&H army disregards the exhibits whose existence they established in the first place. It does not consider or refer to any of those exhibits. For that reason we would like to ask you to look at paragraph 81 of the judgement. In it, the Trial Chamber established that evidence indicates that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in possession of howitzers, cannon, rocket-launchers, in the area of Sarajevo under the control of the B&H army. So howitzers, cannon, rocket-launchers, weaponry for the destruction of armoured vehicles, anti-aircraft guns, different kinds of guns, up to 100 mortars, up to 12 tanks, and vehicle-mounted mortars which moved around the different areas of the town. From footnotes 287, 288, and 289 of the judgement, we can see that we're talking about heavy weaponry which was located in the area of Sarajevo under the control of the 12th Division of the Army of BiH. The map also shows negligible number of mortars or unknown number of mortars, and from the cited evidence, the Court establishes that there were as many as 100 mortar positions. This is something that the Trial Chamber does not even refer to in paragraph 898 of the judgement. I would need to read to you a part of the testimony by Witness Fraser which we quoted in our Appeal Brief, I need to read it here because we find this is very important. He said: "Muslim mortars were deployed in the town and it was extremely difficult for the Serbs to respond to this fire because they were in contact with civilians, they were deployed in civilian environments. This is evidently deliberately done because in the event of counter fire it would have been very, very difficult not to endanger civilians." This is a high-ranking officer and this is his testimony from the time when he was in Sarajevo, based on his experience. And to continue, in paragraph 82 of the judgement, the existence of a factory for the manufacture of shells is established in Ali Pasina Polje, for which the judgement establishes that it is absolutely a civilian zone. Nobody -- it's as if nobody would be going to collect weapons from that paragraph. In paragraph 84 of the judgement it was established that the 1st Corps did not withdraw the heavy weaponry when the exclusion zone went into effect. In all the situations, when it was important, weapons were taken from these depots and used for fire, and this is something that is shown in the evidence and not reflected in the judgement. In paragraph 129 of the judgement, for example, the existence of howitzers is established at positions on Zuc hill. In paragraph 763 of the judgement it is established that there is evidence that the ABiH opened fire from Mojmilo hill, from Hum hill, from Debelo Brdo hill, from Colina Kapa, from Ali Pasina Polje, Igman, Hrasnica, whereby the footnotes refer to a number of exhibits on which this conclusion is based. These are hills where allegedly Serbs had positions. These are elevations at the highest level, whereas the evidence indicates that these were places that were taken up by units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina because they were within this line of separation. However, the top elevations, except the one in Trebevic, were always held by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is something that is indicated in the exhibits. I'm going to refer to some of them if not all. The Serbs were on the other side at the foot of the hills, and this is this misconception that was accepted. We managed -- because we had access to archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina and got these exhibits, we managed to point this out. I must point out these major difficulties that we encountered in the course of our work. From the very beginning of the trial we had acquired more than 4.000 documents from archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was very difficult for us to use these documents, specially during a part of the -- the part of the Prosecution presentation of the case. We didn't have the translation. We translated some parts of the documents ourselves. Many documents that I'm going to refer to today were translated later and then admitted in their entirety. And these exhibits actually indicate what I'm presenting to you today. With a lot of difficulty, however, we did manage to have these documents admitted, we managed to translate them, even though each document was questioned for relevancy. They were relevant because those positions and the fire indicate that these were not civilian areas at all that we're dealing with. Paragraph 129 of the judgement, I've already covered that. Now we're talking about paragraph 764, 765, 766, and 767 of the judgement where there is evidence about heavy weaponry from which the ABiH fired on the territory under SRK control. In the course of 1994/1995, they fired at Grbavica, Rajlovac, Vogosca, and Ilidza. These were also urban areas of the town, only they were under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. And Grbavica, for example, and the area of Nedzarici were a ghetto, they were totally encircled in the heart of the town and this is something that the evidence shows, and we dealt with this in our Appeal Brief so I do not wish to repeat that here. In paragraph 83 of the judgement there is mention of sniper position and sniper weapons. There is also reference to sniper activity of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, paragraph 768 of the judgement. In paragraph 7, General Milosevic said that there was sniper weaponry. The documents indicate that there was sniper activity by the B&H army, but - and this is indisputable - but also there are assertions that every activity or sniper fire from the Serbian forces was directed against civilians -- actually, the activities refer to sniper activities of both the armies. And then we're talking about paragraph 771 of the judgement where evidence is referred to about the fire by the Bosnian government opened -- was opened from a number of buildings and from other locations under the command of the ABiH, such as the Mojmilo, Debelo Brdo hills, the Loris building, Hum hill, and Pofalici. It's similar in paragraph 773 and 774. Paragraph 776 refers to evidence that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina regularly opened fire from different locations throughout the town very often and very close to positions of the United Nations, the building of the PTT, the Zetra sports hall, the Marsal Tito barracks, and that it used mobile mortars. In paragraph 777 we're talking about opening fire from positions which were close to locations of the UNPROFOR. This very evidence stated in the judgement and completely ignored by the Trial Chamber when it came to drawing conclusion on the civilian status on one part of Sarajevo under the control of ABiH completely compromised the conclusions of the first-instance Trial Chamber. These are facts which have been established in the judgement and have not been evaluated in the sense, as I've just pointed out. I'm going to point out to many UNPROFOR -- four UNPROFOR reports. There are many more of them but they have been completely ignored. I'm talking about P19, P39, P519, as well as D3. It arises from the aforementioned pieces of evidence that there was the activity of the artillery of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina immediately in the vicinity of the UNPROFOR facility, but also one can establish the positions of the heavy artillery of the BiH army across the town. This is shown by document or evidence P19. Furthermore, one can also establish that there was artillery fire opened on the 16th and 17th November, 1994, immediately after Dragomir Milosevic assumed his duties. The activities of mortars from the area or even in the vicinity of the building of the Presidency, residence, and the Kosevo Hospital. The evidence also corroborates allegations that fire was opened from heavy artillery in town which constitutes the violation of the zone of total exclusion, as it is stated in the document under P391. Evidence also speaks about fire being opened from the vicinity -- in the vicinity of the building of the PTT and the building of the television. This is in document P519, and that was on the 28th of June, 1995. Furthermore, there is evidence of sabotage fire from the south-eastern suburbs of town as seen in document D3. All of these positions were in the heart of the centre and that's why I mention these four, or rather, three UNPROFOR reports, three of them being Prosecution evidence and one of them being Defence evidence. It arises from the -- or rather, I have just mentioned Exhibit 594 -- P194, which was a map depicting the positions of all the brigades in the territory of the city of Sarajevo under the control of the BiH army. And now I'm going to talk about documents produced by the BiH army which have all been admitted into evidence. I'm talking about decisions, orders, reports on activities, the daily consumption of ammunition. Believe me, for every single day we had proof that there was activity. We tendered some 20 documents which speak about where the weapons were and how many shells were fired on every day. There were days when as many as 1.000 shells were fired, and would you say that this was a civilian zone? These maps always depict the areas of responsibilities of each of the brigades as well as certain areas which have their depth and width and cover the entire area of the city under the control of the BiH army, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, just as the map shows. And it is not only about the 30 command posts, because every command post as -- had its forward command post and observation posts. These documents also show the positions of infantry, artillery, mechanised strength, engineers, communications systems, the positions of anti-aircraft defence and observation posts. You can also see the positions of certain services such as quarter-master services and technical services, as well as the positions of some smaller units, the positions of the military police, or something that was totally outside of the brigade command, even the reconnaissance companies, the positions of logistics structures and their rear bases. You can even show the positions of reconnaissance and sabotage units. One document, for example, issued by the supreme commander Delic, unfortunately we could not bring Delic as a witness. The Trial Chamber did not want to bring him as a witness despite our implorations although he was sitting in the adjacent room. And you can see in that order how his soldiers were supposed to act. I'm going to find the document and I'm going to read from it. The reference is made to destroy, come back - this is in capital letters - destroy and come back, which means go to Sarajevo, destroy something there, and come back. I would like to point out here that apart from the infantry, the positions of other military structures could never be on the separation lines especially not in the trenches, and the Trial Chamber reduces everything to the fact that some or many soldiers were in the trenches and the only thing that they did was that they sometimes went home to rest there. And obviously I'm now in a very difficult position. I cannot, although I'll try as much as the time permits, I'm going to try and show you some of the documents among the documents that show about the positions and the actions and I'm going to try to point to some crucial things. However, I can at least mention the number of each of those documents, and then if you have the time and inclination, you may be able to look at the documents which have all been translated. And you will be in a position to see what they're all about because each of the documents speak for themselves, and they will show you that the conflict had a permanent duration and there was no single day without a conflict. How each of the sides reacted is a subject of a possible evaluation, but first of all you have to establish whether that was a civilian zone. What is being claimed all the time, what is being proven all the time, or attempts were being made to prove that this was a civilian zone - that's the Prosecution case - but I'm trying to tell you differently and it's up to you to evaluate. However, the first thing in order to establish any form of responsibility you have to establish beyond any reasonable doubt that that was a civilian zone, and these are the documents in question: P492, D190. I'm going to read at least one part from P492 because this is a statement provided by General Karavelic. Before this Tribunal we were able to hear only two officers and one foot-soldiers. The only people who were examined were police officers. The Prosecution wanted to demonstrate in that way that in a civilian zone the only people who can testify are police officers, because nothing was happening there; and at the end of the day, the police officers were also experts about the incidents and the things that were happening there, although they directly participated in the fighting all the time. And their credibility is something that should be questioned. This is the only thing I can tell you. However, I'm going to read from this Prosecution exhibit to point to some very crucial things. D417, D418, D426, D195, D194, D270, D398, D423, D413, D463, D462, D110, D163, D118, D154, D219, D107, D494, D428, D423, D160, D416. What follows is a series of documents with -- the admission of which we had a lot of difficulty, although they depict the positions and activities of all kinds of weapons in the territory of the town under the control of the BiH because the Trial Chamber always wanted to question their relevance, and we were in the possession of 4.000 documents of the same kind and we managed to tender only some. And even those that we managed to tender into evidence speak about hundreds of thousands of bullets being fired from infantry weapons and thousands of shells. We did not have enough resources to tender many other documents. These days I would like to mention that, although it may not be important for you, one of the principal newspapers in Bosnia-Herzegovina puts a question - I don't know how they know it - they ask: Where did the Milosevic Defence team obtain all the documents? And they ask for the responsibility of those who provided us with the documents. But it was their duty, and we tendered some which we were able to translate, but they are a good enough illustration of the things that I'm trying to point out. What documents are these? D189, D188, D467, D308, D191, D470, D507, D472, D471, D437, D313, D436, D466, D468, D469, D505, D236, D473, D504, D465, D153, D192. Each of the aforementioned documents speaks about combat activities in one day, and each of the documents shows what kinds of weapons were used, how many bullets were fired. Hundreds of thousands of bullets are mentioned in a single document. These documents also show what heavy weaponry was used, how many shells were fired, but first and foremost they show the positions of the heavy weaponry. In one place in the judgement - I can't remember exactly where, I will remember and I'll tell you - it says that the Defence has not provided a single piece of evidence to show that Sedrenik was a war zone; however, there are nine documents that we have tendered that shows that Sedrenik, which was an urban area in the town, how fire was opened from there on particular days. Those weapons were not in trenches. There is a document saying, Today we opened fire from a distance at Spicasta Stijena. I believe this is document 313, there are some others and maybe I'll have enough time to show them to you. And when I said just a little while ago that document P492 is something that I have to quote from in more detail, and I believe that the time will allow me to do so, and let me remind you that this is the statement provided by General Karavelic, the commander of the 1st Corps. Look what he said? You have that on page 6 of the English version, and I'm saying that this is on page 6 of the English version in the last paragraph of the chapter entitled "Formulating of Political and Military Strategy." And I quote: "When it comes to the defence of certain parts of Sarajevo which seem to be militarily unsustainable, what was necessary was to preserve every single metre. All Sarajevo was of vital importance because we did not have enough manoeuvre area. Every square metre had to be defended irrespective of the military difficulty it may have presented." He is talking about positions on every single step, every single square metre. He's not talking about command positions. And now on page 6 of the English version under the title "Defence Tactic in Sarajevo," this is what Karavelic says: "Our defence tactic had to protect the defenders by digging ourselves as deep as possible. We created two lines of defence with two trenches around the entire perimeter. There were two lines of trenches around the entire city of Sarajevo. Those lines were dug-in down to 2 metres and they also comprised deep shelters and dormitories. The engineers' support or artillery support was the vital factor of defence." A reference is made to defence but now what about offensives. That's an entirely different issue. "In some areas the defence was reinforced by a third line. This was not a line of defence in the literal sense of the word but a lot of strongholds which could be defended in case of a breakthrough. Brigades had one battalion on the front line, one was on reserve and the third was on furlough, and then they would take turns usually every week. The 1st Corps had a manoeuvre brigade in reserve. It did not have its own area of responsibility. It was at disposal for counter attacks as needed, and those brigades were also rotated. The manoeuvre brigades were kept in a very high level of combat-readiness so that they could be rapidly deployed." This means that there were three front lines in-depth. One battalion, as it is described herein -- the entire city of Sarajevo was intersected by positions. And now, please, if that was indeed the case, can such an area with such activities be qualified as a civilian zone? And finally, I believe that I'm duty-bound to try -- I believe I'll have the time to try and point out to some other documents which I believe I should quote from. Can I have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have covered this. I want to refer you to D190. This is an order of the 8th of June relating to the 1st Corps as a whole. There at page 3 of the English version, item 2, mention is made of an activity from a certain stretch of the front line, and then units are mentioned which were supposed to set out from the city. However, more importantly, at page 6, item 6, of the English version mention is made of the fire support and of the precise areas of responsibility, specific weapons and positions, anti-armour combat. Specific positions are mentioned at Sokolje, in specific apartment blocks and houses. I'm constantly referring to the 12th Division, and I simply do not have the time to relate to matters which have to do with other divisions. It is not necessary at this stage. The other document, D417 is also of paramount importance. At pages 3 -- or rather, at page 3 of the English version you will find the specific areas of responsibility as they were positioned in various parts of town. Then you have the deployment disposition, offensive forces, defensive forces, anti-armour combat forces, security forces, commanding forces, forces on stand-by. For instance, for the 112th Brigade you have the exact positions of artillery in the Astra area, the forward command post, et cetera. You will find this in respect of each and every unit and I do hope that you will study the document. Every brigade unit has its own AOR clearly defined -- it is clearly defined which part of the ABiH-held territory is controlled. For instance, guns, at page 7 it's stated in the area of Ciglane, Brescici, Busce, Sedrenik, and Sedrenik is mentioned in the judgement as a purely civilian area. It is stated that we did not adduce any evidence to show whether it was a civilian or a military area. Et cetera. I would need a lot more time to deal with all this. We also have mention of engineering support in the same document, D418, for instance. For the month of March you have the positions of the brigades and the weapons. D195 is something that should be paid specific attention to. The commander of the 101st, who is in the centre of town, clearly details the various positions of weapons on the Heroj Square, Hrast area, Bristol Hotel area. Every piece of heavy weaponry is specifically mentioned here as well as the position where it was located. Document D194 which, towards its end states: "In all the areas of defence of the various battalions, facilities, or rather, firing positions should be created in order to fire over the heads of own units." D270 also speaks of the defence areas in the depth. Then 413 as well. 462 speaks of the sniper fire and the number of fortified position from where fire was to be opened. There was also a number of decoy sniper positions, mock sniper positions. Then you have document P163 where Delic writes to Izetbegovic, the Commander-in-Chief, and says: "We must continue stating that we will be defending ourselves and not attacking first, as we have always been doing. Demilitarisation of Sarajevo is out of the question for the following reasons ..." How can a civilian zone be demilitarised? Can someone explain this? The document is self-explanatory. This is simply unfathomable. Or take only D118: "In the period from the 15th of June until the 3rd of July," in other words, a 20-day period, "we fired from all sorts of weapons at our disposal upon over 300 enemy targets." The document goes on to say: "We believe that the number of damaged combat and non-combat positions is higher because we fired on them in conditions of limited visibility at night where observation was not quite possible." So we're talking about a period of 20 days and it was Fikret Prevljak, the commander of the 12th Division, writing about this. For 20 days there was fire from all weapons at the disposal of the 12th Division. There was another document that I wasn't able to find a moment ago, D219, which says: "These tasks are to be carried out in such a manner that the enemy is made quite unstable and uncertain and the manner in which this is to be done is destroy and return," and this is an order issued by Rasim Delic, who appeared before this Tribunal. Let me not go into the other documents now. This is the sort of documents I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Meron would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, we've been hearing your argument with interest, but I would be grateful to you if you could give us some broader indications regarding the following: When a city -- civilian city's under attack and uses armed forces to defend, does it lose, thereby, its civilian character and become some military objective? And in what situation or constellation of forces would an essentially civilian city retain its civilian status while defending or using armed forces defensively? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have a moment to consult with my learned friend?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a very sensitive issue and I will try to give an answer. The war broke out in 1992. In late 1994 -- or rather, the documents that I referred you to show that in late 1994 this was no longer a civilian area, although there was a civilian population. Through other evidence that I wish to refer you to, I will show to you in answer to your question what the specific situation was when it comes to the civilians themselves. The civilians were unable to leave the town and they were used directly. It is a sensitive issue. This sort of situation that prevailed in Sarajevo in 1994 demonstrates that there was not a house to be found which did not have weapons. Every house was a military target. We have the testimony of a senior officer, Fraser, that I referred to earlier, who said that in a certain way every building was a bunker, that there was not a single building that was not fired from. This has to do with what I mentioned earlier about the positions of the mortars and with what senior representative of UNPROFOR had to say in relation to that. It is a matter for you to decide on, but the question is: Was this a civilian zone or a military zone? This is something that you will decide based on my submissions. I -- we will be trying to present the matter in detail. I do apologise. I am growing a bit tired and I would like to refer you to a number of other pieces of evidence and my time is running out. So -- and to leave me some time to look into the matter that you've asked me about. In relation to this matter, the deaths of soldiers and civilians in the SRK-controlled parts of Sarajevo at Grbavica, Dobrinja, Nedzarici, Lukavica, Vogosca, Ilidza, Hadzici, et cetera, would they have come about had there not been artillery and other sort of fire from the ABiH? Well, this is a question and that's why the finding of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 798 that the deaths of the Bosnian Serbs did not have any bearing on the criminal responsibility of the accused is something that is hard to understand. Of course there was -- were victims on both sides, highly regrettable victims, but their deaths indicate that they could not have been killed had they had a civilian area next to them. There was a high number of civilians killed from artillery fire in the part of town under the control of the SRK, just as there were many deaths of civilians on the ABiH-controlled part of town, simply because this was a result of threats to civilians who should never have been threatened to begin with. It will be up to you to decide whether there is any responsibility as alleged in the indictment when all the circumstances of the armed conflict are taken into consideration. Hopefully I will be able to raise a few other points and I don't think I will be able to cover everything. Let us go back to the victims which are treated in the judgement as the victims of the activity of Dragomir Milosevic. The judgement did not establish beyond reasonable doubt either the total number of victims in the indictment period or even less their civilian status. We will not be repeating what we analysed at great length in paragraphs 100 to 128 of our Appeals Brief. I only wish to say that the way in which the Trial Chamber establishes the causal link between the actions of Dragomir Milosevic and the victims which, according to reports of the Bosnian police allegedly died in the territory of the ABiH-controlled Sarajevo in the indictment period is unacceptable. When we refer to the causal link we primarily had in mind the incidents which the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber believe constituted the crucial evidence that the attack was directed from -- against civilians. In other words, the investigations carried out by that same police which was part and parcel of the forces of the BiH were accepted without any reservations, just as were the findings by Ewa Tabeau, which does not make a distinction between the victims fallen in the ABiH-controlled parts of Sarajevo and the SRK-controlled parts of Sarajevo. She refers to all of them as the victims of the SRK activity in the indictment period. At paragraph 737, it is stated that throughout the war from 1992 through to the end of the war, 1.800 to 2.000 inhabitants perished. However, there are no separate figures for the period covered by the indictment. According to what this paragraph says, one could conclude that the victims fallen in that period amount to roughly 500. Seemingly, the general position of the Trial Chamber was that the -- a civilian zone can only have civilian victims. Despite 60.000 soldiers who were regularly stationed and active in the ABiH-controlled Sarajevo, there is not a single soldier because it was a civilian zone. Even when deceased persons wearing ABiH uniforms transported to the hospital, at paragraph 675 it is concluded that the persons probably perished while buying victuals. Is it possible that not a single victim was to be found who was a member of the armed forces of the ABiH, given the dimensions of the combat activity? According to the judgement - and I want to draw your attention particularly to this - victims were the consequence of combat activities which had always come -- or fire which had always come from the SRK-controlled positions. Whenever the possibility of Sarajevo inhabitants leaving the ABiH-controlled parts of town was discussed in the judgement, it was always stressed that Sarajevo was a besieged town and that every attempt to leave the town carried a risk of death and that the civilians were unable to leave the town in any significant numbers, paragraph 749, or that because of the SRK fire from the hills surrounding the town, the civilians were unable to leave the town under the control of the ABiH, paragraph 417. Your Honours, at this stage I would not like to open the debate about who held the positions on the hills surrounding Sarajevo. I would refer you to our Appeals Brief paragraph 139, which shows that all the hills around Sarajevo, except for Trebevic, were occupied by the ABiH forces, and this is based on the evidence. I don't want to stress too much the testimony of Milorad Katic who spoke of the possibility of leaving Sarajevo, the ABiH-controlled part of it, when the blue paths were open, paragraph 748. However, it is very important to answer the question whether it was only the SRK weapons which led to the victims in the ABiH-controlled parts of the town in the indictment period; or better said, is there any evidence about the activities of the 12th Division of the 1st Corps of the BH army activities directed at their own positions, at the parts of town under their control, and particularly whether such activities caused any victims among citizens, BH soldiers, UNPROFOR soldiers who were in the ABiH-controlled parts of Sarajevo; or is the Trial Chamber's finding accurate to the effect that the only reasonable conclusion that can be inferred from the evidence is that the shots were fired by the SRK, and who should such victims, if any, be attributed to? I'm now going to refer to exhibits that the Trial Chamber did not review at all and it should have done so in line with the legal considerations. These are exhibits D190, D417, D205, D216, D149, D148, D66, D67, D147, D51, and D179, which all describe the same event. The first two documents were not considered at all by the Trial Chamber, and they indicate the existence of a general order to fire on anyone who tries to cross into territory under the control of the SRK. Thus, document D190, I'm going to be precise, dated the 8th of June, 1995, and please if you can look at 9 page, paragraph 9, item 2, line 5, from the bottom of the English version contains the order of Karavelic, the commander of the 1st Corps, which states: "Prevent any attempt of crossing over to the aggressor's side even with the use of fire-arms, not differentiating between soldiers and civilians in this case." If you look at document 4 -- D417 of a few days later, now issued by commander of the 12th Division, Fikret Prevljak, which states on page 11, line 5, from the top of the English version, and it states: "Prevent the crossing of our fighters to the temporarily occupied territory and the use of fire-arms for this purpose is allowed." According to the commander this order refers to fighters. According to the evidence it was acted pursuant to the order of Karavelic and Prevljak. In Exhibit D205 of the 7th of April, 1995, which is the time-period of the indictment, it is stated: "Last night, at 1930 hours, our fighters, from Loris, shot and killed an elderly woman who wanted to cross to the other side." So this is a civilian who was killed even before the previously cited orders and this was obviously a pattern of behaviour. According to Exhibit D216 of the 15th of October, 1994, it says: "At 2015 hours, our guard at Palma noted an escapee who tried to escape to the aggressor's side. The guard opened fire and injured the person." In this exhibit either it is not stated that we're talking about a soldier. According to Exhibit D419 of the 6th of April, 1995, signed by Karavelic himself, it is established that in the evening hours fire from a fire-arm prevented an attempt of a person to cross into Grbavica. It does not say that there was a soldier in question here. Only in Exhibit D148 of the 14th of October it says that one soldier was fired at who attempted to cross over to the side under the control of the VRS. Now we're -- could you please specially pay attention to Exhibit D66. This is a letter by Alija Izetbegovic sent to General Delic of the 22nd of April, 1994, and it states, France -- he had visited the French ambassador who had informed him about these events and he says that France is angry because of the killing of one of its soldiers in Dobrinja. Delic -- the ambassador informs Delic that the military expertise indicates that the soldier was shot from positions of the Bosnian army and that the French were not permitted to conduct an investigation or to have access to all the positions from which the soldier could have been shot. In the document it is stated that the French ambassador informed Izetbegovic that he had evidence that out of the 24 soldiers who were killed from their UN contingent, over one-half of those killings were committed by the B&H army. Exhibit D67 establishes that one UNPROFOR officer, after an investigation was conducted, established that a tram in the centre of town was fired at from the Muslim side and he specifies precisely the building from which fire was opened. We indicated about this in our Appeals Brief that in a large number of cases, according to witnesses, citizens of Sarajevo were fired upon from positions of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is even an exhibit from the 3rd of November, 1994, about fire opened at the Bosnian Prime Minister, Mr. Salajdzic, from positions under control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Such fire by the B&H army on their own citizens was confirmed by witnesses Harland and Nicolai before the Trial Chamber, and this is cited in paragraphs 104 to 115 of the Appeal. Such fire from infantry weapons at a section of the town under control of the B&H army and the killing of their soldiers, the soldiers of UNPROFOR and civilians, the Trial Chamber in paragraph 774 considers among specific cases of sniper action by the B&H army against the Bosnian Serbs. I apologise for speeding a little bit. And perhaps if any of those 40.000 citizens of Sarajevo, the Serbs under the control of the B&H army, tried to leave that area they could have been among them. This is a complete distortion of the facts. The evidence indicates that the B&H army did not permit anyone to leave town from parts that were under their control and such -- any such attempt was prevented by fire. These were not rumours circulated by members of the SRK, but these were facts established by indisputable evidence, documents of the B&H army themselves. This indicates that many victims in the areas under control of the B&H army in Sarajevo were casualties of fire by that same army. And the victims were always ascribed to the SRK. The Prosecutor began their case with the case of little Nermin Divovic as the most drastic crime committed by Dragomir Milosevic. What does the evidence actually establish? Among other things, the autopsy findings that we had at our disposal were only about that case and indicate that he was hit by a shot that came from the B&H territory. Of course we dealt with that in paragraphs 184 to 224 of the appeal. We allow you to assess that. There is only one piece of evidence about this in the case of this infant and it indicates that it was not one bullet that killed two people, but we're talking about two bullets that killed that person. We deal with this in specific paragraphs of our appeal in more detail in order to prove precisely that this child was not killed by a bullet fired from positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, but we're leaving this for you to evaluate. The evidence that we indicate seems to -- present seems to indicate beyond doubt that the B&H army fired at their own people, and these are not rumours. Well, if we were going to deal with the case of Markale and the television building case and some other incidents, I would be able to indicate to what an extent this all would remain in the sphere of not being established beyond reasonable doubt. Considerable doubts remain and I would need several days to prove something like that, and that is not possible here in this case. In any event, for artillery fire it is not true that the most that can be concluded on the basis of the facts presented was that there were rumours primarily launched by the SRK that the B&H army shelled civilians who lived in the territory of town under the army B&H control and staged incidents in order to secure sympathy of the outside world. So that would seem to indicate that there was not one single victim, either among civilians or among soldiers of the B&H army or the UNPROFOR in the area of town under control of the B&H and that that any person had been killed as a result of artillery fire by the B&H army. However, in the judgement the actual Trial Chamber in paragraphs 433 and 437 establishes the following. Paragraph 433: General Fraser, Brigadier-General Fraser remembers that on the 18th and 19th of September, 1995, in an interval of 40 minutes, two attacks were carried out by -- on the town by mortars. In each incident shells had fallen on exactly the same part of town and the number of civil -- casualties was twice as large. It indicates that projectiles arrived from two different directions, one from the SRK-held territory and the second rounds came from Bosnian Muslim-held territory. Paragraph 437, it says, and this is again in reference to rumours only and insinuations. The French said that they had seen soldiers of the B&H army filming a staged attack on children in which no one was actually hurt for broadcast on television. And then David Harland says this: Bosnian Muslims in Sarajevo, in reference to the media when it was desired to create media events, they had to create these conditions for that to happen and this is how some of these shootings came about. The judgement itself indicates that these were not just rumours circulated by the SRK on artillery actions by the B&H army on their own positions and that events of the 18th and 19th of September, which fall into the indictment period, indicate that the B&H army, firing on their own positions, doubled the number of casualties. This double number of casualties, to whom should they be ascribed? Either to the shelling of the Bosnian army that fired on their own positions or something else. Another example that we refer to indicates that the B&H army was able to stage incidents for media purposes. In paragraph 185 of the judgement witnesses W-138 and 137 established that there were cases when evidence on the scene was altered or even placed. Another witness, a high-ranking officer of UNPROFOR recalled that shelling incidents when UN investigators were not allowed access for hours to the scene of the incident, and once they did, they found evidence that could not have been a consequence of fire by the Serbs. This witness said that the possibility of manipulation had to be taken into account. So in all of these cases these were not rumours and insinuations but specific evidence about the staging, manipulation, and killings by B&H army. In other words, there were victims that had nothing to do with fire by the SRK but they were always ascribed to the SRK. We have two photographs, D370 and 371. They show two victims of shelling that allegedly struck the Markale market on the 28th of August, 1995. The Trial Chamber accepted explanation by expert of Milosevic that fragments were not the only means that can kill a man at the site of an explosion, and we agree. So thus, on the list of casualties of Markale, one victim was a victim of shot fired from a -- buck shot fired from a hunting rifle and another victim was killed by a rifle bullet even though we're talking about a shelling incident here. This is only possible if there is manipulation with the casualties in the way explained by the top-ranking officer of UNPROFOR. These photographs that we're talking about, it is possible - and I have a lot of experience in these cases, I've handled similar cases, so only if there is manipulation with the victims. I would like to finish, Your Honours, before the break. If I am permitted I would like to say a few words about an event of which Dragomir Milosevic was acquitted. This is the water line. Why he was acquitted. The judgement constantly refers to shooting of the waterlines, parks, and so on, but they did not manage to prove one single incident. This only one incident about the waterline he was acquitted of. Am I allowed to say a few more words about the television building and Markale, and I believe that I am sticking to the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I believe we have to make the break also for the interpreters and for the tapes. So I believe we break now and we reconvene at 11.15 for the continuation of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We resume the hearing and we will give the floor to the Defence to complete their submissions until 11.45. May I urge the Defence to take into account the questions that have been put by the Appeals Chamber to the parties and answer them. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours. I will do my best to address several matters in a couple of minutes if possible at all. When mentioning victims I cannot but mention document D415. When we're talking about victims in the territory of Sarajevo controlled by the ABiH between 1992 and the end of the war, how are we to treat the 15 individuals referred to in the special brief of the security administration of the staff of the Supreme Command of the ABiH? And that's precisely the exhibit I mentioned. When referring to victims, the Trial Chamber speaks of a figure ranging between 1800 and 2.000 for the entire period of the war between 1992 and 1995. However, the Prosecution never adduced any evidence as to the number of victims relevant to the indictment period. This particular document I refer to indicates, and that's D415, that there were most heinous crimes committed in Sarajevo. A body -- or, rather, some 15 bodies had been exhumed in this context, and these were thousands of victims whose deaths will be a matter of prosecution before some of the courts in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. And perhaps these 15 victims referred to in this special brief will be among them. A moment ago I mentioned artillery fire. This had to do with the events of the 18th of June, 1995, and that's the Simon Bolivar school incident. Accused, Dragomir Milosevic, was acquitted in respect of that incident. However, what the matter involved was that - and this is quite important - not a single shrapnel was found at the crime scene. And according to what the police established, there was several victims. The Trial Chamber accepted the explanation whereby the shrapnel disappeared in the air or were blow away. But then how did it come that the victims who were on the ground perished from shrapnel? As for the TV building, in that incident, at the very start of the trial a very serious piece of evidence was presented to the effect that the aerial bombs had not flown in only from the area under the control of the ABiH, but that the ABiH army had such bombs. I'm referring you to D103 where UNPROFOR representatives who were in the area throughout the period themselves testified that the aerial bombs had been fired from the ABiH-held territory. The Trial Chamber invested a great deal of effort to disprove the document even though the UNPROFOR representatives who gave a statement in relation to this stood by what they had said. It has not been established beyond reasonable doubt that the events surrounding the TV building happened as they were described in the judgement, in other words, that the fire came from the VRS-held territory, since the ABiH had in possession that sort of weaponry as well. A word about the Markale incident. We dealt with the matter in our Appeals Brief at great length, but what I wish to say now is that the Trial Chamber found that there were a great many disputable issues in relation to the incident. Despite that, the Trial Chamber inferred the conclusions that it did, even though the radars did not detect the shell, even though it was found that the damage that was inflicted could not have been inflicted by one shell only. According to paragraph 767, 12 shells had landed into a wedding party in front of a church and only one individual was injured, and 12 shells had landed. Here only one shell caused the death of 40 persons -- 50 persons. We led evidence to the effect that the explosion came about in static conditions. According to documents D10, D85, D118, and D186, these are confidential documents of the UN, the charge was very questionable. In Markale I, it was not enough to take care of the azimuth and angle of descent. The charge should have been taken into consideration as well, because without having established the charge of the shell, the distance that the shell flew could not have been established, and in fact the distance was not established. It was a static explosion and not a single piece of evidence led to this day established the distance from which the shell was fired. I may have a few points to make after my learned friends' submission. What I wish to state here and now is that it was not established beyond reasonable doubt that the area of Sarajevo was a civilian area. There is a plethora of evidence indicating that it could not have been the only and absolutely the only reasonable conclusion on the one hand, and on the other, on the issue of civilian victims who perished the way I described and the status of these victims, I can say no more at this point. But if one element, a required element for the establishment of this crime has not been established, namely, that this area of town was a civilian area, then the conviction against my client on this score cannot stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Madam Judge, Your Honours, I'm now going to address you. I can hear something in my headphones, very bad, very disturbing. I need some time to arrange my documents. You addressed in your order four very specific issues. Allow me not to follow the order you took them in because I'm first going to address the first issue, then the third and the fourth, and Mr. Tapuskovic will provide you with some arguments regarding the second question you raised. As to the first issue, as we understood it you want us to say more about the elements of terror or, as was done by the Appeals Chamber in the Galic case, the only known -- or case law known to the Defence in this Tribunal regarding this crime you mentioned acts or threats of violence whose primary purpose is to spread terror among the civilian population. The Trial Chamber in the instant case - but I do not have a French translation of the trial judgement which is somehow regrettable because we were working in French. Furthermore, it is one of the official languages in this Tribunal. But the Trial Chamber mentioned terror. In French it's "terrorisation." This is therefore the term we used in our Appeal Brief. Regarding the elements of this crime, let me first of all express our amazement, surprise, given the order followed by the Trial Chamber in their trial judgement now under appeal. Towards the end of the judgement it is a very muddled way regarding the way the elements for the crime are considered because there are two elements for the charges. First of all, there is a section III (A), count of terror. Thereafter, they follow the orders 1, 2, 3 in numbers, and then it is surprising to have under "Terror," murder, inhumane acts, and then later on the trial judgement speaks of the individual criminal liability of the accused. All this was very difficult to understand, to find the right position, to understand the Trial Chamber's reasoning. But that was our job and we wanted to provide you with the way we understand the Galic case law, which is, in our view, in keeping with what you have done. Let me quote -- then we gave further details in our Appeal Brief but we took paragraph 0104 [as interpreted] of the Galic appeal judgement that told us which were the elements that constituted the offence, but you also have a footnote 351 in the Galic judgement and it shows clearly what your position was regarding the charge of attacks on civilians in relation to the alleged crime of terror. "Terrorisation" in French, to make it short. Indeed, in footnote 351 under paragraph 110, let me quote part of it: "Terror is a crime that encompasses attacks on civilians, therefore this part of the judgement applies mutatis mutandis to the finding of guilt by the Trial Chamber -- by the Appeals Chamber against Galic for threats of violence, the primary purpose of which is to spread terror among the civilian population." The Defence kept in line with your Galic jurisprudence, and this is the way we analysed the alleged crime of terror; in other words, we took the material element, the actus reus, which is expounded in detail in our brief, and acts or threats of violence directed against the civilian population or against civilians not taking part directly in hostilities. So further to this, further to this analysis, afterwards we analysed the evidence and we were bound to look again at this same -- or in -- at the evidence that the Trial Chamber totally disregarded or used for a totally different purpose legally speaking or carried out a legal analysis that is, in our view, totally different from what you said in the Galic appeal judgement. So we took up the evidence, analysed it, and used all the relevant indicia in order to demonstrate specific facts which are indispensable if one is to enter a conviction for the crime of terror. Regarding the mental element of the offence, we took the parts that we found in your jurisprudence as well as in the authorities that are regularly used by this Tribunal. And it can be said that the crime of terror and for it to be constituted to be made out and for its material element to be made out you have to prove not only the intent to carry out attacks against civilians not taking part in hostilities but also to show a specific intent, a specific intent, the primary purpose of which is within attacks on civilians to spread terror among civilians or among the civilian population as a whole. So this is the way we interpreted your jurisprudence, especially based on the mens rea, the mental element of the offence. We considered that the approach of the Trial Chamber -- you see during closing arguments questions were put to the parties. The parties were invited to assess the evidence in the case file, the evidence on the record, whilst this should be the primary job of the Trial Chamber, and the parties were asked to give a definition of "terror." One member of the Prosecution team was asked to define terror and it must be also said that this definition - and this is said by us in our Appeal Brief - this definition encompasses an assessment of the evidence indeed. The Prosecution speaks of terror as felt by the civilian population. Therefore, the Prosecution assesses the evidence, although they're no psychologists and they did not call an expert on the matter. And thereafter, the Trial Chamber decided to apply the Prosecution's opinion in order to establish Dragomir Milosevic's intent to spread terror among the civilian population. We do not agree with such an approach, not at all. Furthermore, we received the Prosecution's response and it was very upsetting because it disturbed all the knowledge Mr. Tapuskovic has. He has 45 years of experience. I've been a lawyer for a little more than 20 years and it really disturbed and contradicted our knowledge of criminal law. In paragraph 65 of our -- of the Prosecution's Response Brief, the Prosecution speaks to the issue of the mens rea and says: [In English] "In fact since it is reasonable to infer that persons intend the consequences of their acts, the Chamber correctly found that the actual infliction of terror could serve as evidence of the intent to terrorise." [Interpretation] I don't know whether this disturbs you as well, but for me, that was the end of criminal law and of the question of evidentiary rules in criminal law because if the consequence is meant by the author, he has the -- the accused has to defend against the fact that he did not have this intent. So this is reversing the entire philosophy of criminal law and this is equally reversing the jurisprudence established in this Tribunal. As far as I'm concerned regarding the elements of the crime, I have no further observations. You may have questions right away; if not, I can move to the second issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't forget that you just have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll now turn to the second issue -- rather, third in the order of the Scheduling Order. It has to do with the use of the elements as aggravating factors. Here again it's quite obvious to us. These are basic predicates of criminal law. You cannot use a situation -- I may turn to the judgement -- all the circumstances that were such that he was or that he is there where he is now, yes, he was a commander, and based on the indictment and the trial judgement he failed to comply with laws and customs of war. But all these are threshold standards -- I mean, requirements for him to be an accused in a trial proceedings.
