You cannot use the same circumstances in order to say, Of course this is a further aggravating factor because he was a commander, he commanded, he failed to comply with the laws and customs of war. So this was impermissible in our view. This is a purely legal point of view. And I'm sure that you will rule on this matter. Now, as to the fourth question, which is more a matter of fact, you asked the parties to supply you with evidence that is likely to show that with regard to the direction established by the Trial Chamber as the origin of fire, that there were positions of the ABiH. The first document I'd like to speak about has been mentioned in our Appeal Brief, D102. It is a map that was marked by a witness Ekrem Suljevic. He was a police officer in charge of the investigation into the matter, and he marked with an arrow the direction. And this was accepted by the Trial Chamber in their factual findings. So at our request, during cross-examination, he marked the positions around the arrow. And this shows that Colina Kapa is close, is in the vicinity as well, and we claimed that there were ABiH positions on Colina Kapa. D110, D417, and these are exhibits I'd like to show you and I also would like to show you some testimony. I couldn't find all the witnesses, but there was W-12, transcript pages 3039, 3042, 3065. Then we had witness Huso Palo, transcript page 1545 to 1546. Witness Thomas Knustad, transcript page 2025, 2026. Witness Vahid Karavelic, transcript pages 4228. utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, your time has expired. I can give you five minutes to end your pleadings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. I believe that the time will be enough because it remains for us to answer another question of yours which regards the alibi. In that respect I believe that I can be brief and I would like to thank you for the additional time that you've just given me. In paragraph 155 we state that the Trial Chamber, in their conclusions under 975 and 976, prevents the application of the general principle of law which envisages that a complete inability of action relieves the person of criminal responsibility. It seems that such an impossibility, according to this Trial Chamber, in order for the person to be acquitted has to last a certain period of time. This is what was stated in paragraph 155 of our appeal. It seems that we are here on the ground of a complete [indiscernible] of the significance of an alibi. If for -- the existence of an alibi is corroborated by everything that was established beyond any reasonable doubt because in paragraph 10831 [as interpreted] it is stated that witnesses have confirmed that the accused was absent while he was in Belgrade and the command duty was taken over by Colonel Sladoje, the Chief of Staff of the SRK. And then in footnotes which you requested we mentioned documents 892, 908, document 733, 732, and another one 734. These are all orders which were signed and issued by Cedo Sladoje in view of the fact that this was not just a simple absence from the scene. The gentleman was sick, undergoing a surgery in a different state, so it was proven beyond any reasonable doubt that he was physically impossible to perform the duties. In such a situation, the Trial Chamber arrived at the conclusion that in practical terms he did not even have to be there in view of what was happening. And then it says in paragraph 976: "The Trial Chamber notes that the absence of the accused from Sarajevo did not last very long." How long it should have lasted? He was absent for five weeks and then returned in Sarajevo. In that respect I have to emphasize something else. From the beginning of September, after the NATO bombing, until the very end of September and then throughout October and November, those are the periods that the Trial Chamber did not evaluate. At that time there was no conflict among the separation line. For three months there was no single incident as a representative example of the campaign. He returned to the scene and together we -- with UNPROFOR he did everything possible to regulate things on the ground. I don't understand how anybody can issue a new legal position about an alibi. An alibi can cover one, two, or three days, and how can somebody say that since Markale happened during that period of time while he was in hospital, completely absent from the scene. Does this mean that three months, for example, would be enough? What standards are those? These are absolutely new standards that annul the traditional institute of criminal law as is practiced here. In addition to all of these documents, Your Honours, once we received your instructions for the appeal, on the 13th of July we tried once again to write a letter to some organs in the state. And from the state we managed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, I would like to seek some clarification by asking you a question. You gave two reasons: To gain the sympathy of the media, you said, or to highlight or to double the number of casualties. Would you be so kind as to expand on this. utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I understand your question. I cannot talk about the intentions of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We gave you some examples, showing that the BiH army, according to the findings of the Trial Chamber itself, manipulated the bodies and artillery fire. I've already stated that. I don't -- I'm not in a position to tell you what the BiH army intended. However, there is indisputable evidence to the effect that there were two orders, one dated 8 June 1995 and another one issued on the 11th of June. The first one was signed by the commander of the 1st Corps, who says that nobody must cross over to the opposing side and that everybody should be shot at if they even try to leave Sarajevo. And the second repeats the same. And I also gave you some documents which shows that the soldiers of the BiH army opened fire. These are facts. Your Honours, these are facts that show that such things happened. What their intention was, why they did what they did, we heard the reference to a lot of things, but I don't want to speculate. Before you I can only state the facts and these were the facts which I pointed to by documents of the BiH army. What the intention was is a different story. There is a theory which says that the Army of Republika Srpska opened fire at everybody, but this was not proven by any piece of evidence. And we had documents showing that there was a blanket order for nobody to be allowed to leave Sarajevo alive on the one hand and we have some particular documents that show it. I've presented them. And as for the event I can't speculate. I could, but I'm not such a person or such a lawyer who manipulates with speculations. Whatever I said was said based on the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution will respond to the Defence appeal in the following way. I will first give an overview over the case and the Prosecution's response. And in that context I will address Your Honours' questions, number 2 and 3 contained in the addendum to the Scheduling Order. My colleague Francois Boudreault will then address Your Honours on question number 1 and our response to Dragomir Milosevic's ground number 1. My colleague Matteo Costi will conclude the Prosecution's submission by addressing ground 8, subground 2, the shelling of the Bascarsija Flea Market, and in that context, he will address Your Honours' question number 4. With regard to the rest of our submissions, we rely on our brief but are available to answer any additional questions Your Honours might have. The Trial Chamber properly convicted Dragomir Milosevic of the crimes of terror and of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please switch off other unnecessary microphones in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber properly convicted Dragomir Milosevic for the crime of terror and for murder and other inhumane acts as crimes against humanity. From August 1994 to November 1995, Major-General Dragomir Milosevic was the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the SRK. And as commander of the SRK, he planned and ordered a campaign of shelling and sniping against the civilian population of Sarajevo. He willingly continued what had started under his predecessor Galic in 1992. Milosevic's troops shelled and sniped at the trapped civilian population over 14 months. As a result, many civilians were killed and injured mentally and physically. Milosevic intended to terrorise the civilian population and he achieved his goal. In the words of the Trial Chamber: "The inability to escape from this trap of horror ... left deep and irremovable mental scars on the population as a whole." Trial judgement 910. Milosevic made sure that no one would ever feel safe anywhere in Sarajevo. Milosevic's snipers deliberately shot at civilians. The snipers targeted places where civilians gathered. They shot at a woman in her bedroom, a women gathering firewood, a mother and her 7-year-old son trying to cross the street, a girl on her way to school, passengers on trams. Milosevic also directed the SRK to shell civilians. Shelling was aimed at civilian areas, markets, places where civilians queued for water. The targeting of the civilians was deliberate. Mortars were accurate weapons and their crews highly trained. But Milosevic did not limit the shelling to mortars, but repeatedly made use of modified air bombs, blatantly inaccurate weapons that could only be directed at general areas. It was impossible to predict where they would strike. An air bomb is ordinarily dropped from an aeroplane, but here the SRK attached rockets to air bombs and fired them from improvised systems such as the back of trucks. Their use in Sarajevo shows that the intent was to terrorise the civilian population, and the Trial Chamber found so at paragraph 912. Milosevic's legal and factual challenges to the trial judgement should be dismissed in their entirety. His many factual challenges must fail. Throughout his appeal, Milosevic repeatedly re-argues his trial submissions. He points to evidence fully considered by the Trial Chamber or offers merely a different reading of the evidence without showing that the conclusion the Trial Chamber drew was one that no reasonable Trial Chamber could reach. In the evidence this morning, Milosevic mostly focused not on the specific incidents that the Trial Chamber was dealing with. As we have set out in our Response Brief, the Chamber carefully considered the relevant evidence, paying particular attention to the source of fire in each incidence. In the case of Nermin Divovic, which was addressed this morning, the Trial Chamber addressed the question of the alleged contradiction with regard to the source of the fire and resolved then that Nermin was shot by a member of the SRK. And I refer Your Honours more particularly to our Response Brief paragraphs 113 through 119. Where the Chamber was not convinced that the SRK was behind the attacks it acquitted Milosevic, such in the last two sniping incidents. In relation to sniping incidents, the Chamber always sought to identify the status of the victim and the context in which his or her activity was carried out. Concerning shelling, the Chamber was careful to assess the circumstances of the attack, the type of weapon, and the status of the victim. Further, when addressing the specific sniping and shelling incidents and whether they were directed at civilians, the Chamber also examined whether there were legitimate military targets in the vicinity. Regarding the legal errors, Milosevic fails to show that the Chamber erred to his detriment in its legal assessment on the elements of crime and the standard of proof. And the Chamber carefully assessed Milosevic's criminal responsibility for planning and ordering. The Chamber correctly found that Milosevic planned and ordered a campaign of shelling and sniping over 14 months. And I will come to Your Honours' question number 2 in a moment, but before addressing the question in detail, I would like to address how the Chamber concluded that Milosevic was responsible for planning and ordering during this period, including the five weeks when he was absent from Sarajevo. The Chamber found in trial judgement 960 that Milosevic, the Main Staff of the VRS, and Mladic were involved in devising the greater strategy for Sarajevo. And Milosevic was able to implement this greater strategy in a manner that he saw fit. The Chamber found that Milosevic planned and ordered the campaign of shelling and sniping in Sarajevo. The incidents of shelling and sniping fit in a pattern contemplated and implemented by Milosevic, trial judgement 978. The Chamber found a design, a consistency, a pattern that was only explicable on the basis of a system characterised by tight command and control, trial judgement 966. And Milosevic did hold tight command over the SRK, trial judgement 959. The sniping occurred over an extended period of time in different areas of Sarajevo under the control of different SRK brigades. This shows that the operation of snipers was coordinated at the command level. This led the Chamber to the only reasonable conclusion, that Milosevic planned and ordered sniping activities, trial judgement 962. The Chamber concluded that shelling of the civilian population was also planned and ordered by Milosevic. He decided on the use of mortars and on the methods of shelling, he requested air bombs, he ordered the quantity of air bombs to be issued to the SRK brigades, he ordered the construction of air-bomb launchers for modified air bombs, and he stated in a report that air-bomb launchers are used throughout the SRK zone of responsibility as required and as decided by the SRK commander, that's trial judgement 963 and 964. The Chamber further relied on planning and ordering of specific incidents as evidence of the plan and ordering of the campaign of shelling such as Milosevic's order regarding the shelling of Hrasnica on the 7th of April, 1995, trial judgement 964. And in fact, the Chamber found that Milosevic went beyond the general planning of the campaign of shelling and sniping. He also took care of details. He was actively engaged in a number of matters, trial judgement 959. He issued numerous orders relating to training, equipment, and deployment of snipers, trial judgement 962, and the Trial Chamber used that evidence to infer that he planned and ordered the sniper activity as such. Milosevic also issued a number of orders relating directly to shelling incidents and I mentioned already the order in relation to Hrasnica. On 19 April 1995, Milosevic ordered all units to launching pads and aerial bombs ready for firing on town, that's trial judgement 834. On 16 May 1995, Milosevic ordered the Ilidza Brigade to prepare aerial bomb launchers to be ready to fire at his command, with launchers being roughly aimed at the airport, trial judgement 835. The general plan and orders by Milosevic remained in place and continued to be implemented during the time -- the five-week period from the beginning of August, when he was absent from Sarajevo, trial judgement 977. Therefore, the Chamber correctly found that he was liable for planning and ordering during that period. When analysing the period of his absence, the Chamber concluded that the ongoing shelling fell squarely within the overall plan and general orders given by Milosevic, 977. And the Chamber recalled that he had full control over the SRK troops, trial judgement 975. It further considered, in paragraphs 976 and 977, that the period of absence was not very long, only five weeks, that it fell in the latter part of his tenure as SRK commander, by then the shelling and sniping had already been going on on his orders for about a year, and during his absence the shelling and sniping continued in the same manner as before. The Chamber found that before Milosevic had left for medical treatment there was an increase in fighting due to ABiH offensives and Milosevic's response to these offensives was shelling of civilian areas within the confrontation lines. And during his absence the shelling continued in the same manner, trial judgement 977. The Chamber correctly concluded that, in the words of the Chamber, "his responsibilities had been taken over by the SRK Chief of Staff Cedomir Sladoje" did not change his liability for planning and ordering. And in the addendum to the Scheduling Orders, Your Honours have asked us to point to evidence on the record concerning the nature of the appointment and the mandate of Cedomir Sladoje during Milosevic's absence. During Milosevic's absence, Cedomir Sladoje, the deputy commander, was in charge, was in the B/C/S terms "zastupa komandanta." Although, to our knowledge, there is no document in evidence setting out the appointment and mandate, the way he signed the orders during Milosevic's absence confirms was with "zastupa komandanta." And the English translations for these orders on the record is: "For commander," "in lieu of commander," "commander represented by." And I refer Your Honours, for example, to the order of the 24th of August, 1995, Exhibit P768, an order from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps issuing units with air bombs; an order on the 7th of September, 1995, Exhibit P734, an order in relation to the return of air bombs to Pretis; an order on the 7th of September, 1995, Exhibit P734, an order from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps relating to further combat action. And I would like to refer Your Honours to Exhibit P738, that is a letter Milosevic wrote to Mladic in 1996 and it's quoted in part in the trial judgement in paragraph 806, but I would like to refer Your Honours to a different part of that letter, it is on page 3 of that letter and I quote: "As soon as I was off for surgery at the VMA (military medical academy) an order was written for one to become NS (Chief of Staff) but it could not be done for me before that." And the B/C/S version of that also refers to "zastupanje." In relation to this word "zastupa komandanta," it was referred to in a different context by Witness Gagovic, and he referred to it as "stand-in commander"; that's transcript page 8699. The Trial Chamber found in paragraph 959 that Milosevic was the de jure commander of the SRK during the indictment period and the Trial Chamber there does not make an exception for the period of his absence. Milosevic's absence was only temporary. The expectation was that he would come back, and he did come back. And I refer Your Honours to the evidence of Luka Dragicevic. Luka Dragicevic was the assistant commander to Dragomir Milosevic from December 1994 onwards, in charge of morale, religion, and legal issues. He was thus in a position to give evidence about the circumstances of Milosevic's medical leave. Dragicevic testified, on transcript page 3999, that they had great difficulties to talk Milosevic into leaving for his eye treatment, to have the problem with his eye resolved so that he could continue his work. As explained by Defence Witness Major Stevan Veljovic, during Milosevic's absence his deputy, Cedomir Sladoje, was in charge. Major Stevan Veljovic was an operations officer, that's trial judgement 466. He was the direct subordinate of Cedomir Sladoje, transcript page 5765. Thus he could also speak about the relationship between Milosevic and Sladoje. And when Veljovic was asked on transcript page 5843: "And who was in charge of the corps when Dragomir Milosevic went for treatment in Belgrade?" Veljovic answered: "His deputy, Colonel Cedomir Sladoje." And the inference on the basis of the totality of the evidence that Sladoje was instructed by Milosevic to continue the campaign of sniping and shelling. This is consistent with the Chamber's conclusion that the ongoing shelling and sniping fell within the overall plan and general orders given by Milosevic. This brings me to the mandate of Cedomir Sladoje. Three factors linked to the inference that Milosevic instructed Sladoje to continue the campaign of shelling and sniping. First, Milosevic's style of leadership and his general attitude as the commander. Second, the continuation of shelling and sniping in the same manner. And third, Milosevic's reaction, or rather, lack of reaction on his return. First, Milosevic's leadership style of tight command supports the conclusion that he discussed with Sladoje what to do during his absence and instructed him to exercise the command to continue the campaign of shelling and sniping. This is supported by Veljovic's testimony. According to him, the two of them always coordinated the approach. Thus, it was not being in charge in the sense that Sladoje could do whatever he saw fit, but rather how it was discussed with Milosevic. When Veljovic was asked by the Prosecution on transcript page 5831: "So it's probably fair to say that he was the alter ego of the commander. They were very close to each other. Because if the commander was away, was absent, if somebody [sic] happened to him, he has to be able to take over at any time?" Veljovic answered: "Yes. And the two of them always coordinated the actions and how the command and control was going to be performed." Instructions by Milosevic are further supported by the fact that he did not leave for the medical treatment on an emergency basis. He had been wounded already in May and the treatment had been put off due to the situation at the front. I refer Your Honours to trial judgement 829 and the medical file of Dragomir Milosevic, that's Exhibit D340, page 4. Instructions are also consistent with Milosevic's general attitude towards his role as commander. This attitude was expressed in the letter to Mladic I already mentioned that Milosevic sent in 1996, and this part is quoted in trial judgement 806. Milosevic writes: "I never stayed away from my troops a single day." This attitude is also supported by the testimony of Luka Dragicevic, who testified on transcript page 3999 that Milosevic even cut his sick leave short. Second, what in fact happened during Milosevic's absence is further evidence that Milosevic instructed Sladoje to continue the campaign of shelling and sniping. The Chamber found in judgement 977 that the shelling and sniping continued in the same manner as before. More specifically, Milosevic's response to the ABiH offensives in 1995, before he left, was to shell civilian areas within the confrontation line. This finding is consistent with the evidence of David Harland, that retaliation was principally directed against civilians, trial judgement 757. And as the alter ego of the commander, Sladoje must have been intimately familiar with the strategy implemented by Milosevic. Further, on 15 July 1995, thus before Milosevic left for medical treatment, he requested the Main Staff of the VRS to approve the issuance of 200 air bombs, trial judgement 822. Having ordered 200 air bombs, the inferences that Milosevic discussed with Sladoje, how they should be used, particularly in light of his tight command. On 10 August 1995, thus shortly after Milosevic had left, the SRK command with an order signed by the head of the artillery, ordered the preparation for the manufacturing of air-bomb launchers, that's Exhibit P731. And on 22 August, a modified air bomb was in fact launched. The BITAS building was shelled with a modified air bomb, trial judgement 668. And on 24 August 1995, Sladoje ordered issuing units with air bombs, signing "zastupa komandanta," "for the commander," Exhibit P768. The shelling against civilians thus continued in the same manner. Third, further evidence that Sladoje acted on Milosevic's instruction is the lack of Milosevic's reaction when he returned, and this despite the fact that according to the evidence of Colonel Dragicevic and Major Veljovic, Milosevic would have been informed about what happened during his absence on his return, trial judgement 832. This evidence supports that Milosevic -- the evidence supports that Milosevic never reported a violation of international humanitarian law to the military prosecutors. Colonel Dragicevic testified that he never learned or heard of any instances where the accused reported a violation of IHL to the military prosecutor. And he also testified he would have been informed about such a report, trial judgement 862. In conclusion, the Trial Chamber reasonably concluded that it was irrelevant for the criminal responsibility of Dragomir Milosevic for planning and ordering that he was absent during five weeks from Sarajevo. This concludes our answer on question 2, and unless Your Honours have any question in this regard, I would turn to the answer to question 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I assume we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you. In its assessment of the gravity and aggravating factors, the Chamber took relevant considerations into account without counting the same factor twice. Rather, the Trial Chamber relied on different aspects under gravity and aggravating factors. This, in short, is our answer to Your Honours' third question which I will now address in more detail. What can be considered under gravity was correctly stated by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 989, referring inter alia to the Galic appeals judgement, paragraph 409. There the Appeals Chamber said that the inherent gravity of the crime, the criminal conduct of the accused, a consideration of the particular circumstances of the case, the crimes for which the accused was convicted, and the form and degree of participation form part of the assessment of the gravity. The Blaskic Appeals Chamber in paragraph 683, also relied upon by the Milosevic Trial Chamber in paragraph 990, further lists the consequences of the crimes for the victims. And in addressing the inherent gravity, the Milosevic Trial Chamber relied precisely on those factors in paragraphs 991 through 994. In paragraph 991, it addressed the mode of liability, planning and ordering, that is, the form of participation; the types of crimes, terror, murder, and other inhumane acts; the seriousness of their crimes and their frequency, when it said all of these crimes are very serious and were committed during a campaign of sniping and shelling over a period of 14 months. Frequency is one of the factors which the Galic appeals judgement in paragraph 410 confirmed as a valid consideration to assess the gravity. In paragraph 991, the Chamber further addressed the circumstances of the case, the environment in which the civilians found themselves: Trapped inside the city. And the Chamber took into account the effects on the victims: Many were killed and seriously injured. In paragraph 992, the Chamber focused on the particular gravity of the crime of terror due to "an intent that is particularly indicative of a disregard for human life and integrity." It further addressed the immense suffering of the civilians during this period. In paragraph 993, it properly considered the fact that terror had been caused, the civilian population was actually terrorised, which is not required as an element for the crime of terror. And the Chamber also recognised that the suffering resulting from actual terrorisation is an element of the crime of inhumane acts. Paragraph 994 sums up the gravity by addressing the modes, the types of crimes, their frequency, and the victims. Turning to the aggravating factors. When addressing the aggravating factors, the Chamber took into account different aspects than what it had considered under gravity. Although in some instances the Chamber used similar wording, the focus under aggravating factors and gravity was on different issues. When addressing the aggravating factors, the Chamber was mindful of the fact, and said so explicitly in paragraph 995, that a factor that had already been taken into account under gravity could not be additionally taken into account as an aggravating factor. Under aggravating factors the Chamber took into account circumstances relevant to measure Milosevic's criminal responsibility, factors which it was thus entitled to use as aggravating factors. In paragraph 999, the Chamber took into account as an aggravating factor: Milosevic's abuse of his high position of authority as corps commander through systematic violations of IHL. The Chamber was mindful that the superior position as such cannot be used as an aggravating factor and it said so in footnote 3202, but the Chamber did not take into account the superior position as such, the authority to give orders, but the abuse of it from a very high position in the VRS in a gross and systematic way. And it is exactly this repeated breach of the public duty from a very senior position that the Appeals Chamber in Galic in paragraph 412 accepted as an aggravating factor for Galic, who, like Dragomir Milosevic, was convicted for ordering terror through a campaign of shelling and sniping. The last sentence in paragraph 999 shows that it is the abuse of this position as an aggravating feature counted here, not a second counting of the modes, planning, and ordering or the violations of the IHL. Rather, those are the ways in which Milosevic abused his position, but the modes as such and the crimes as such had already been taken into account under gravity in paragraph 991 and summarised in paragraph 994. In paragraph 1.000, the Chamber considered the duration of the campaign, Milosevic's willing continuation of it, and his very active role in the commission as aggravating factors. The length of time during which the crimes continued as well as the active and direct criminal participation, if linked to a high-rank position of command, have been accepted by the Blaskic appeals judgement in paragraph 686 as aggravating factors, and were correctly listed by the Trial Chamber in this case in paragraph 996 when describing the law on aggravating factors. The reference under gravity in paragraph 991 to a period of 14 months is in the context of seriousness and frequency of the crimes merely descriptive, not counting the duration as such. Further, 991 under gravity relates to the frequency of the crimes, whereas the focus in paragraph 1.000 is on the conduct of the accused. In paragraph 1.001, the Chamber correctly considered the highly inaccurate nature of the modified air bomb, coupled with the great explosive power to be an aggravating feature. When the Chamber, in paragraph 1.001, refers to the psychological effect of the modified air bomb, it focuses on the effect of this weapon. This is a different aspect from the reference to the immense suffering under gravity in paragraph 992 when the Chamber refers to the overall effect of the campaign of shelling and sniping. In paragraph 1.001 under aggravating factors, it was the choice of this weapon and its repeated use that the Chamber found to be aggravating. Using a blatantly inaccurate weapon with great explosive power is not an element of the crime of terror so that the Chamber did not impermissibly count it twice. In conclusion, the Chamber considered correctly the circumstances under gravity and aggravating factors without counting the same factor twice. This ends our response to Your Honours' question number 3, and unless Your Honours have questions, I would pass on to my colleague Francois Boudreault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Ms. Goy, there are no questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So you can proceed as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOUDREAULT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will be addressing question 1 of the addendum to the Scheduling Order. I will also address briefly the arguments raised by Milosevic this morning in relation to grounds 1 of his appeal and show why they must be rejected. Question 1 of the addendum to the Scheduling Order invites the parties to elaborate on the elements of the crime of terror. The Prosecution's position is that there are three elements. First, the acts or threats of violence; second, the direct or indirect intent for these acts or threats of violence; and third, the specific intent to spread terror among the civilian population. In the present case, the Trial Chamber also required a showing that the acts or threats of violence caused death or serious injury to body or health within the civilian population. This is at trial judgement paragraph 875, 876, and 880. We submit that this is an error. As I will show in a moment, the Appeals Chamber did not endorse such a requirement in the Galic appeals judgement. Before I turn to this, I would emphasize that the error of the Trial Chamber does not affect the outcome here because the Trial Chamber did, in fact, find that the SRK attack had resulted in death and serious injury to civilians. This was a reasonable conclusion, as we explain in paragraph 56 to 60 of our Response Brief. Further, the fact that civilians were killed or injured as a result of the SRK attacks actually reinforces the Trial Chamber's conclusion that these attacks were directed against the civilian population of Sarajevo and that the specific intent behind these attacks was to spread terror among the civilian population. I now turn to the Galic appeals judgement. Paragraph 102 of the Galic appeals judgement explains that the acts or threats of violence constituting the actus reus of the crime of terror can comprise attacks or threats of attacks against civilians, and that it may also include indiscriminate or disproportionate attacks or threats thereof. But the Appeals Chamber does not find that the acts or threats of violence must result in death or serious injury to civilians, even though this was clearly in question, as can be seen from the discussion preceding paragraph 102. At paragraph 100 of the Galic appeals judgement, the Appeals Chamber notes that the Galic Trial Chamber had described the actus reus of terror as "acts of violence ... causing death or serious injury to body or health within the civilian population." However, the Appeals Chamber does not endorse this requirement. At the end of paragraph 100, the Appeals Chamber specifically notes that the Galic Trial Chamber did not consider whether the actus reus of terror could consist only of threats of violence or acts of violence not causing death or injury. Paragraph 101 of the Galic appeals judgement then explains that the analysis of the elements of the crime of terror must be based on the definition of that crime in the Additional Protocols, that is: "... acts or threats of violence, the primary purpose of which is to spread terror among the civilian population." The Appeals Chamber then discusses the actus reus of terror at paragraph 102, which, as I just said, makes no mention of a result requirement. The Appeals Chamber thus found that a showing of death or serious injury to civilians is not required for the crime of terror. This is consistent with the fact that the primary concern with this crime is the specific intent to spread terror, Galic appeals judgement, paragraph 102 to 104. Our learned colleagues referred this morning to footnote 351 of the Galic appeals judgement, however, that footnote says nothing about the elements of terror. It only provides an explanation as to why in the specific case of Mr. Galic there are challenges to the findings with respect to the counts of unlawful attacks on civilians. This interpretation of the Galic appeals judgement is also shared by the jurisprudence of the Special Court for Sierra Leone. The Appeals Chamber and the Trial Chamber of the Special Court have all followed the Galic appeal judgement on the actus reus of terror. None of them has required proof that the acts or threats of violence constituting terror caused death or serious injury to civilians. I would refer in particular to the Fofana appeal judgement at paragraph 350 to 352, and to the Sesay trial judgement at paragraph 117 and footnote 240. Incidentally, the Special Court considers that attacks on civilian objects could also constitute the actus reus of terror. The Prosecution's position is thus that a conviction for terror does not require a showing of civilian casualties. That is not to say that any act or threat of violence can constitute the actus reus of terror. The acts and threats of violence in question must be capable of causing extreme fear in the targeted population. This is in accordance with the third Tadic requirement that the violation must be serious. The Appeals Chamber of the Special Court for Sierra Leone has also found so at paragraph 352 of the Fofana appeal judgement. In the present case, the Trial Chamber thus erred in requiring proof of death or serious injury for the crime of terror. As I explained, however, this error does not affect the outcome here because the Trial Chamber did reasonably find that the SRK attacks had resulted in death or serious injury to the civilians. This concludes our submissions in response to the first question. I'm available to answer any questions you may have in this connection. Then I will say a few words in response to Milosevic's arguments this morning on ground 1. The Trial Chamber was well aware of Milosevic's argument that there were military targets within Sarajevo, but it reasonably found that the SRK attacks discussed in the judgement were directed against civilians. Milosevic attempts to obfuscate these findings by arguing that the SRK targeted military zone, but international humanitarian law does not speak in terms of military zones. What the law states is that civilians and civilians -- civilian objects cannot be directly, indiscriminately, or disproportionately targeted. This is a fundamental principle that applies in all circumstances. I would refer you to Blaskic appeal judgement paragraph 109, Kordic appeal judgement paragraph 54, and the Galic appeal judgement, paragraph 130. The presence of military objectives in an area does not change anything to this. This is confirmed by Article 51(5)(a) of Additional Protocol I which prohibits an attack "which treats as a single military objective a number of clearly separated and distinct military objectives in a city, town, village, or other area containing a similar concentration of civilians or civilian objects." So to come back to the question that was asked earlier by Judge Meron, a civilian population can never become a military target. Of course, civilians can be killed or injured as collateral and proportional damage in relation to a lawful military attack, but they cannot be directly or indiscriminately targeted. Here the Trial Chamber was well aware that Sarajevo contained military objectives and it considered all of Milosevic's arguments. It dealt with the allegations that the ABiH occupied the elevations around Sarajevo, it dealt with the allegations that the ABiH staged incident or that it fired on its civilians. It also dealt with the arguments that the Bosnian police was part of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it nevertheless found that in the specific incident, civilians or the civilian population were directly or indiscriminately target by the SRK. The civilian casualties were not simply a mistake or collateral or proportional damage resulting from legitimate military attacks. Milosevic fails to address the specific findings of the Trial Chamber and the evidence on which these findings are based. In grounds 1 and 6 of his appeal he simply refers to general evidence that there were military objectives in Sarajevo. This is insufficient to show that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable in finding that the SRK targeted civilians in the specific incident discussed in the judgement. Grounds 1 and 6 should be rejected. This would conclude our submission in response to ground 1 of Milosevic. As before, I'm available to answer any questions on this ground or on grounds 2 to 4, 6, and 12 of Milosevic's appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: There is no question. You can proceed -- well, depends on what follows. If it remains within the 15 minutes, the next argument, we can take it now; if it's longer, we have to break now inevitably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I was going to suggest was that Mr. Costi can deal with the question 4, Bascarsija Flea Market incident, and then invite Your Honours to rise and if there are any other matters we wish to take up, we'll take them up after the break. If we do take anything up, I don't anticipate we'll be very long with it. So Your Honours can be thinking of adjusting the schedule and truncating it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. So perhaps Mr. Costi may take the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I will deal now with the shelling of the Bascarsija Flea Market on the 22nd December 1994. I will divide my submission in two parts. First I will answer Your Honours' question. And second, I will briefly respond to the appellant's argument that the Trial Chamber needed to determine the charges of the shell in order to find beyond reasonable doubt that the origin of the fire was in the SRK-held territories. I will begin by answering Your Honours' question number 4, and I quote: "Discuss the evidence on the trial record, if any, that supports or rebuts the allegation that the shells may have originated from the territory controlled by the ABiH in the same direction." The short answer: There is no evidence on the record supporting the allegation that the shells that hit the Bascarsija Flea Market on the 22nd December 1994 may have originated by the ABiH. The evidence we heard this morning cited by my learned colleague from the Defence only show that the source of the fire in the SRK-held territory was in the same line of the ABiH territory, being a city under siege this is almost always the situation. The evidence on the record, actually, positively support and rebut this allegation. The Defence assertion that the ABiH were responsible for the shelling and sniping in Sarajevo was discussed and rejected at trial. During trial the Defence questioned several witnesses on the possibility that the ABiH troops were firing on their own people to gain the sympathy of the international community. The Defence even suggested that some of the attacks were staged. Now, the Trial Chamber considered and rejected these allegations, also in light of the exhibits and that were quoted this morning by the Defence, and decided, if you let me quote, Your Honours, the trial judgement at paragraph 795 that: "In relation to the Defence allegation that the ABiH shelled Bosnian Muslims living within the confrontation lines, the Trial Chamber notes that it heard no such evidence. Instead, the Trial Chamber heard evidence from a number of witnesses, including UN officials, that the ABiH did not shell their own population. The Trial Chamber further notes that the allegation about the ABiH staging the incidents for propaganda purposes or to gain sympathy was not supported by the evidence showing that such cases actually occurred. The Trial Chamber finds that the most that can be made of the evidence presented is that there were rumours primarily from the SRK side." So the Trial Chamber did find that the ABiH never fired on its own people in Sarajevo. Now, consistent with this finding, the Trial Chamber reasonably concluded that the ABiH did not fire on its own people at the Bascarsija Flea Market on the 22nd December 1994. In doing this, it relied upon the specific evidence of the BiH police investigations and the testimony of W-12. Dealing first with the police investigation. The Trial Chamber heard the testimonies of three police officers that participated to the investigation. The police, under the supervision of an investigative judge produced a 91-page investigative dossier, which is Exhibit D124, and concluded that the shells were not fired by the ABiH but from the south-east SRK's position on Mount Trebevic, and this is Exhibit D124 at pages 1 and 3. Now, the solid conclusion of the police is based in particular upon two elements: First, the testimonies of 15 eye-witnesses, four of them were specific in indicating that the shells came from Mount Trebevic, Exhibit D124, pages 6, 7, 22, and 25. One of them who was about 500 metres from Vidikovac when he witnessed the event, stated that the shells were fired from Vidikovac on Mount Trebevic. Vidikovac was the upper part of Mount Trebevic held by the SRK. The second element on which the police relied upon in its conclusion is the analysis of the crater, the crater left by the shells. This indicated that the direction of the shells was south-east 159 degrees, corresponding with the direction of Mount Trebevic. And again I refer to Exhibit D124, P310, P315, and P275, under seal, and I would also direct Your Honours' attention to transcript page 3119. The result of this analysis was confirmed by the independent investigation of the United Nations Military Observers, the UNMO, at Exhibit D101, page 2, and P833, page 6. Moving now to Witness W-12. W-12 was a member of the ABiH, a Bosnian soldier deployed on the south-east front line in Sarajevo. When the shells were fired he was on the slope of Mount Trebevic in the area of Brajkovac, near the confrontation line. He was walking with five other persons towards the ABiH positions. On his right, below in the valley, was Bascarsija, the old town of Sarajevo. On his left, above him, was Vidikovac, on the upper part of Mount Trebevic where the SRK's position were. He heard the explosion of the shell being fired. And in essence, he stated that the shells were fired from Vidikovac and he was sure they were not fired by the ABiH because the highest ABiH positions were much lower than the source of the sound. These are transcript pages 3039, 3047, and Exhibit P308. I would refer also to Exhibit P306 and 307, both under seal. He then heard the shell landing in Bascarsija. Bascarsija is an area he knew very well because he lived in the neighbourhood, in Bistrik. He explained that from the position where he was that morning, on the slope of Mount Trebevic, he could hear what was happening below in Bascarsija. And again I would refer to Exhibit P306 and 307, both under seal, and transcript pages 3038, 3039, 3041, 3048, and 3071. Now, the appellant cross-examined W-12 in order to challenge his credibility, and I would refer Your Honours' attention to transcript pages 3061, 3068, 3076 to 3078, and today, in his appeal brief, only repeat the same challenges. But the Trial Chamber heard and observed W-12 first-hand and found him to be a reliable witness, not only in relation to this incident but also with respect to other matters. In assessing his credibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Costi, can you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I am very sorry. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Apparently the translation cannot cope with the rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I am sorry also to the translators. I was saying that the appellant had the chance to cross-examine W-12 and in his Appeal Brief he is basically re-arguing the same challenges already before the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber heard and observed W-12 first-hand and found him a reliable witness. In assessing his credibility, the Trial Chamber had also the opportunity to observe, during a site visit, the locations of Bascarsija, Mount Trebevic, and Vidikovac. The task of hearing, assessing, and weighing the credibility of the witnesses is for the Trial Chamber. And the appellant has failed to show an error on the part of the Trial Chamber in how it assessed the evidence of these witnesses. Your Honours, as the Trial Chamber found, there is no evidence suggesting that the ABiH ever turned its weapons to fire its own people -- on its own people. The evidence on the record rebuts this allegation and supports the Trial Chamber conclusion that it was not the ABiH who fired the shells that hit the Bascarsija Flea Market but it was the SRK under the command of Dragomir Milosevic. Now, if you have, Your Honours, any questions on this point or if you want I can ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: There is no question, unless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: President, I would like to ask a question which the Prosecution could answer after lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I would like to return for a moment to the Prosecution's argument that -- or contention that particular acts or threats do not require death or serious injury to civilians to qualify as a crime of terror. I would be grateful if you would explain after lunch perhaps how does your contention fit into the holding of the Galic appeals judgement. And as a subsidiary question, if death or serious injury are not required, is a psychological damage or traumatic damage required? You might want to reflect on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sure, Judge Liu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I also have a question concerning the paragraph 999 of the judgement which take the commander position of the accused as an aggravating factor and convicting him as planning and ordering him to gross and systematic violation of the international humanitarian law. To my understanding that the element of ordering requires that somebody in the position of authority to request or make somebody to commit a crime. Do you think that the Trial Chamber double counting that position in authority as an aggravating factor? And of course you said not, but I want to hear you elaborate on this aspect. You may answer this question after we come back in the afternoon. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, this concludes the hearing of this morning. We will reconvene as scheduled, at 2.15 or perhaps 2.30. 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.59 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, we resume the hearing. At the end of the morning some questions had been put by Judges to the Prosecutor, and the Prosecutor would like to answer these questions now. Before they do, perhaps may I add an additional question, additional to what has been asked by my colleagues, Judge Meron first, on the crime of terror. If I'm correct, the Prosecution referred earlier to the elements of the actus reus of crime of terror, arguing that in order to satisfy the third Tadic condition, the acts or threats of violence alleged should be such that are at the very least capable of spreading terror. The Prosecution observed also that in Galic terror should be understood as the causing of extreme fear. Now, in light of this submission is perhaps the Prosecution arguing that actual terrorisation of the civilian population is a requirement of a crime of terror which was not recognised by Galic? If not, I would like perhaps the Prosecution to elaborate on how an act that is merely capable of spreading terror but does not actually do so will satisfy the third Tadic condition, in particular which will be the grave consequences for the victims. So perhaps in answering you may take this point also into account. Please, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. We suggest to proceed in this way. I will first very briefly finish my submission in relation to the Defence eighth ground of appeal. Then my colleague Francois Boudreault will address Judge Meron and President Pocar's question, and finally, my colleague Barbara Goy will address Justice Liu's question. So I will briefly respond to the appellant's eighth ground of appeal. The appellant argues that the Trial Chamber needed to determine the charges of the shells in order to be able to find beyond reasonable doubt that the origin of the fire was in SRK-held territories. Now, it is true that in the same direction at the foot of Mount Trebevic, below the SRK offensive position there was the ABiH line of defence. And it is also true that the Trial Chamber made no findings on the calibre or the charges of the shells. However, the Trial Chamber was fully entitled to conclude, on the basis of the totality of the evidence discussed before, that the shells were fired from the SRK-held territories. Now, let me, Your Honours, be clear on this point. The result of technical analysis of the incidents, such as the determination of the calibre or the charges of the shells, are not fact indispensable to the conviction to be proven beyond reasonable doubt. They are nothing more than helpful indicia that, when present, can be taken into account together with the evidence to determine who fired the shell. What needed to be proven beyond reasonable doubt on the totality of the evidence is that the shells were fired by the SRK, and this is exactly what the Trial Chamber did and found on the basis of the police report, the UNMO investigations, and the testimony of eye-witness W-12. Your Honours, the appellant has failed to show that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have concluded that the shells that hit the Bascarsija Flea Market on the 22nd of December, 1994, were fired by the SRK. Now, Your Honours, before I conclude I would like only to address one last point. This morning the appellant listed a series of exhibits that in his submission would show that the ABiH fired on its own people in Sarajevo. And this contrary to the Trial Chamber finding at paragraph 795. We reviewed during the break these exhibits and we submit that none of them show that the ABiH troops were firing their own people within the confrontation line. For instance, if I may, just very briefly Exhibit D148, and it's just one among the other, it says -- it is a letter of the Bosnian Herzegovina command, Army of the Bosnian Herzegovina command and it says that: "On 14 October 1994, one of our soldiers tried to escape to the other side, in Grbavica sector. Our soldiers opened fire and probably wounded him." Now, I won't go on reading others, but the point is that, first of all, that all this evidence were before the Trial Chamber, most of them are quoted in the judgement. Second, none of them supports that the ABiH ever fired at its own people within the confrontation lines. And third, and more importantly, none of them refers to the shelling of the Bascarsija Flea Market. So this would really end my submission unless there are any questions from Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Boudreault, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOUDREAULT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will respond to Judge Meron's question and then I will address Judge Pocar's question. Your Honour, our position is that the Galic appeal judgement does not impose a result requirement. Terror does not require proof of civilian casualties or psychological or traumatic damage. If you would allow me to take you through the Galic appeals judgement starting with paragraph 100, which ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOUDREAULT
utterances.text: If you could turn on the video on your screen. Yes. At paragraph 100 of -- is it working? If I could direct your attention first to paragraph 100 of the Galic appeals judgement. The Appeals Chamber first outlines the elements of the crime of terror as identified by the Galic Trial Chamber, the first one being the: "Acts of violence directed against the civilian population or individual civilians not taking direct part in hostilities causing death or serious injury to body or health within the civilian population." At the bottom of paragraph 100 of the Galic appeals judgement, the Appeals Chamber explained that the Trial Chamber did not consider whether it would have jurisdiction over forms of violence other than acts of violence causing death or serious injury; that is, it did not consider whether the crime of terror against the civilian population could consist only of threats of violence or acts of violence not causing death or injury. The Appeals Chamber then explains at paragraph 101 that the analysis of the elements of the crime must be based on the definition provided in the Additional Protocols. At paragraph 102 the Appeals Chamber explains that the acts or threats of violence constituting the actus reus of terror can comprise attacks or threats of attacks against the civilian population but may also include indiscriminate or disproportionate attacks or threats thereof. The Appeals Chamber then explains in the middle of the paragraph at page 50 that the primary concern with the crime of terror is the specific intent to spread terror among the civilian population. Towards the end of the paragraph the Appeals Chamber explains the distinction between terrorism outside of an ongoing military attack and the war crime of terror, the crime with which it is concerned. It says that the crime of terror is concerned with "'extensive trauma and psychological damage' being caused by 'attacks [which] were designed to keep the inhabitants in a constant state of terror.' Such extensive trauma and psychological damage form part of the acts or threats of violence." In our submission, this excerpt simply describes the type of harm sought to be prevented by the prohibition on terror. In other words, it describes the type of harm that must be intended by the perpetrators of terror. Our submission is that the Galic Appeals Chamber did not seek to impose a requirement to prove extensive trauma and psychological damage. Such a result requirement would be difficult to reconcile with the Appeals Chamber's subsequent discussion at paragraph 103 and 104, which finds that the actual terrorisation of the civilian population is not an element of the crime of terror. Your Honours, we say that extensive trauma and psychological damage is terrorisation in that context. Requiring proof of extensive trauma and psychological damage would be to require proof of actual terrorisation. This was rejected at paragraph 103 and 104 of the Galic appeals judgement. Turning to Judge Pocar's question, as I've just mentioned, we do not dispute that actual terrorisation is not an element to be established. We nevertheless think that acts or threats of violence which are capable of causing actual terrorisation in a population satisfy the third condition of the Tadic decision; that is, they involve grave consequences for the victims. In particular, as the civilian population is put in danger by these acts or threats of violence and as it is deprived of its sense of security. Some of the more concrete threats that may be or more concrete consequences for the victims that may follow from this, the attacks or threats of attacks will profoundly affect the way civilians lead their lives. To take the example of the case at hand, the civilians were forced to live underground, to avoid crowds, to get out only in night, to forego some of their activities. In brief, their entire life was affected by those acts and threats. The acts and threats might even force civilians to leave the area. So these are certainly serious and grave consequences for the victims. Your Honour, this would conclude our submission. Unless there are further submissions, I will pass on to Ms. Goy.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will conclude the Prosecution's submission by addressing Your Honour, Judge Liu's question posed before the break with regard to the aggravating factors addressed in trial judgement paragraph 999. In paragraph 999 the Trial Chamber did not double count an element of the mode of liability of ordering, the use of the position of authority. Rather, the Chamber took into account Milosevic's abuse of his very high position of authority as corps commander through systematic violations of international humanitarian law. The position of authority, as Your Honour Judge Liu has rightly pointed out, is inherent in the mode of liability of ordering and as such cannot be used as an aggravating factor. But here it was not even the mere abuse by issuing orders, but the abuse from a very high position of authority. And the last sentence of paragraph 999, where it says "abused his position," has to be read in context with the rest of the paragraph, where the Chamber held that "Milosevic held one of the highest positions within the VRS. He had a special responsibility to uphold standards of IHL." And in Galic the Appeals Chamber had accepted this as an aggravating factor. In paragraph 412 of the Galic appeals judgement, the Appeals Chamber has accepted as aggravating the repeated breach of Galic's public duty from a very senior position, and Galic was in the same position as Milosevic, corps commander of the SRK, and was also convicted for having ordered terror through a campaign of shelling and sniping. The Chamber therefore here did not count the authority to give orders, not the mere abuse of ordering as such, but the abuse from a very high position of authority in a gross and systematic way. This concludes our answer to Your Honour's questions, and unless there are any further questions this also includes the Prosecution's response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, then I take it that the Prosecution has concluded its response. I will turn now to the Defence for the reply. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honours. I shall reply briefly to questions I have already answered. In light of what the Prosecutor has said, I shall begin with the question that has to do with the consideration of similar circumstance, i.e., the elements of the crime as aggravating factors. In our view, this is extremely clear. We only discuss the errors in law committed in paragraphs 999 to 1001 and -- and the answer was given to your question, we -- our answer was more of a legal nature. We do not deviate so much from the Prosecutor. Should we not consider the prerequisites and then increase the sentence of a convicted person? What is being discussed is the abuse of authority of a commander. The way we put our case is that our client is innocent, but theoretically speaking, if we were to consider the abuse of authority, can one imagine for a single second that a commander commits crimes, war crimes, without abusing his authority. This is a conundrum which, to all intents and purposes, is rather difficult to imagine. As far as the issue, question number 4, is concerned, the incident that took place in the flea market of Sarajevo, the Prosecutor recounted what is contained in the judgement. We understand full well that he agrees with this, but we developed this in paragraphs 239 to 261 of our Appeal Brief and we clearly indicated that this incident was an isolated incident. And we demonstrated that it has not been proven beyond all reasonable doubt that the only possibility in these circumstances was to conclude that the shots came from the positions held by the SRK. This is precisely the standard that is applied before this Tribunal. We have explained all of this in detail in our Appeals Brief, more specifically in paragraph 251, and the Prosecutor told us earlier that it did not need to demonstrate that all the indicia, i.e., the charges, range, and all the elements needed to be proven. But these indicia we feel need to be proven, because according to the case law of the Tribunal and Ntagerura appeals judgement we need to, and the Prosecutor has a duty to prove this beyond all reasonable doubt, all the relevant indicia to determine the culpability of the accused. This was not the case because, let me remind you, that it was important to determine the charge of a projectile. The direction is not enough. When you have a projectile flying in both -- in the same direction from the same warring faction, you need to demonstrate the charge of the projectile which is one of the indicia which is in line with the jurisprudence in Galic, which is perfectly well explained. And all this needs to be proven. So I'm not going to spend time on Witness B-12 [as interpreted], on the basis of which all of this rests, because there are some unanswered questions in this regard and this is what we discuss in our Appeals Brief. At the end, this is the last but not the least, the elements of the crime of terror. Whilst I listened to the Prosecutor and when I listened to the questions that were raised, I'm a little bit afraid of the Galic appeals judgement being reversed. I hope this is not going to happen because a question of your competence to rule on the crime of terror is raised. At no point in time was this the case put by the Defence, and precisely, if I'm not mistaken, the Tadic case law was designed to demonstrate that as part of Rule -- Article 3 of the Statute, certain crimes can be tried even though they are not listed. We agree, nonetheless, that the crime of terror, as it is described in the Protocols and in your case law, is of -- falls within the competence and jurisprudence of this Tribunal. So to re-assess the gravity of the offences seems to me a little bit far-fetched, but we will see what is to happen after your deliberations. Now, what is being brought up again is the Galic appeals judgement. We forget to say -- and a while ago I was referring to this footnote which illustrates this perfectly well. So what comes to mind is a question of legal rationale. Why could there not be a cumulative conviction for civilian attacks and the crime of terror if one accepts what we are being told today, namely, what has been said by the Prosecutor? In other words, the actus reus is identical between the two; the mens rea, i.e., the crime of attacks against the civilians, and in addition the specific intent to spread terror. The Prosecutor told us in its Response Brief that the fact that terror is spread is not included in the actus reus. I cannot look at this right now, but this was mentioned again by the Prosecutor today because terror that is inflicted, i.e., really spread, actually spread, is not an element of the crime. This is something we explained in our Appeals Brief because the intent must be proven and there are a number of criteria to be met. This is mentioned in the Galic appeals judgement, not by terror or fear or the spreading of terror among a population or a civilian population or individuals taken -- or civilians taken individually. This was explained. We can conceive that a commander sees that there are attacks against civilians, the primary purpose of which is to spread terror, but then if nobody is afraid, is that person held liable for that crime or not? One can also imagine that the civilian population is terrified by the war that surrounds it, that is perfectly normal. But nonetheless, it must be proven on the basis of other indicia that these attacks had for sole purpose to spread terror and made it so felt on the civilian population. These are the questions which to my mind are essential questions and I'm sure and I hope that you are going to apply the Galic jurisprudence in this field. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.
