utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. Your Honours, I'll be dealing with the Prosecution's appeal against sentence. Your Honour, the Prosecution's primary submissions in this case are that the Trial Chamber erred in crediting, first of all, Dragomir Milosevic with any mitigation in this case; and secondly, that it erred by imposing a manifestly inadequate sentence of 33 years' imprisonment instead of life to reflect the role of the accused, the seriousness of the offences, including the impact on the victimised population of Sarajevo. As a preliminary matter, Your Honours, the Prosecution has advanced an argument in its brief at paragraph 21 that the Trial Chamber failed to count as the victims of terror persons other than those who were the victims of sniping -- of the specific incidents of sniping and shelling. On one reading of paragraph 993 of the judgement, that does seem to be what happened, but at paragraph 910 the Trial Chamber also referred under "Terror" to the - and I know Your Honours have already quoted it - "deep and irremovable mental scars on the population as a whole." And it may be, therefore, that Your Honours consider the Trial Chamber did have in mind the effect of the campaign of terror on the entire population of Sarajevo when sentencing. And, Your Honour, obviously I leave it with Your Honours as to what you make of that. Your Honours, I turn now to deal with the appeal. On the 18th of November, 1994, within the indictment period, Dragomir Milosevic was 52 years of age. He had risen to the rank of major-general in what had become the VRS and had assumed command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps by latest 12th of August, 1994. On the 18th of November, 1994, Nermin Divovic was 7. The evidence does not record where Dragomir Milosevic was on that day. Perhaps he was visiting his troops, something Your Honours have heard he did regularly, earning, according to Defence witnesses, the high esteem of his soldiers because he took care for their needs, trial judgement 805. The trial judgement does record where Nermin Divovic was, 325 to 341 in the judgement. He was with his mother, Dzenana Sokolovic, and his 8-year-old sister. They were in the besieged city of Sarajevo, walking home on Zmaja Od Bosne, or Sniper Alley -- do Your Honours have any difficulties with the translation because mine suddenly went to French on the English channel, as it were? Your Honours, I'll go back. The judgement does record where Nermin was. They were in the besieged city of Sarajevo walking home on Zmaja Od Bosne, Sniper Alley, close to the Holiday Inn. They had collected firewood from Hrasno, 4 kilometres from their home in Bistrik. As they approached Franje Rackog Street where it met Sniper Alley, Nermin was talking to his mother, holding on to her jacket. At the end of the street, across the Miljacka River, inside the Metalka building, were SRK snipers. Nermin and his mother would have been unmistakable from the building, yet one of those soldiers shot them. The bullet passed through Nermin's mother's body leaving her with significant physical scarring, and then passed through Nermin's head killing him. John Jordan, an international firefighter and rescue worker, who attended many such incidents said of them: "When you are targeting civilians like this, particularly families who may or may not be a Muslim, shooting the child has the effect of literally disembowelling the whole family." Trial judgement 747, transcript 2697 to 8. That day, the 18th of November, 1994, was typical in Sarajevo, when SRK snipers under the command of Dragomir Milosevic stole the lives of its civilians. They took them on the trams and while going to work, when collecting water and gathering food, on the streets and in their homes. They left the survivors stripped of their dignity and their emotions, leaving them numb to grief and to the pain of loss, running everywhere, living in basements, hiding behind makeshift screens. In the words of Martin Bell, recited in the judgement at para 275, they "looked haggard, they looked hunted. Survival was what it was about. They were truly desperate times." As if this sniping was not enough, SRK troops shelled and bombed those civilians trapped inside Sarajevo intending to kill them, to cause them serious bodily injury, trial judgement 932, and to terrorise them, trial judgement 967. Offensives launched by the city's defenders often resulted in the civilians being punished with retaliatory shelling and sniping, reference trial judgement 757. At the apex of the SRK sat Dragomir Milosevic. Between about the 10th of August, 1994, and the 21st of November, 1995, he presided over, planned, and ordered the implementation of the campaign of sniping, trial judgement 962 and 966, and shelling, 964 and 966, begun while he was deputy commander to General Galic. His purpose in planning and ordering this campaign was to terrorise the civilian population, that is, to create extreme fear, trial judgement 883, over and above that experienced by civilian population in close conflict. In this he succeeded. The entire population of Sarajevo had inflicted deep and irremovable mental scars on the whole population. One witness trial judgement 3236 -- sorry, forgive me, transcript 3236, trial judgement 811, described the SRK activities under Dragomir Milosevic as "more subtle," "more precise," and "more dangerous" than those of his predecessor General Galic, now serving a life sentence imposed by this Chamber. Brigadier-General Fraser testified that there was "a commander's intent in play around the city of Sarajevo with respect to the sniping incidents." To him the sniping along Sniper Alley in the centre, around the airport to the south-west, and Spicasta Stijena to the north-east, indicated a "higher commander's intent." Trial judgement 853. In developing this campaign Dragomir Milosevic continued to shell Sarajevo with mortars both deliberately or indiscriminately. Both the Bascarsija Flea Market and the Markale market were struck. At Markale there were extensive casualties, 34 civilian deaths, at least 78 people wounded, many seriously, some losing their limbs. The judgement at paragraph 675 recites by way of example the statement of Mesuda Klaric, P648, who was 55 and in the street by the Markale market with her husband Ismet when the shell landed. She described the immediate aftermath, and I quote: "... it was like I was half conscious ... I saw my husband grab his right arm. Then he told me 'I lost my arm' ... I was covered with blood everywhere ... I saw a lot of people laying on the street ... a car stopped and one young man grabbed me ... another stopped ... they picked up my husband ... the young man put me in his car, together with a young girl and another young man ... the young girl lost her foot." She saw her husband had lost his foot and had a groin injury through to the bone. He and her husband were admitted for surgery. The last time she saw him was as they took him to the morgue. She continues to have shrapnel in her back near her kidneys and in her knee. She ends her statement in this way: "All the wounds are now healing, except that my husband is gone." In addition to Dragomir Milosevic's mortar shelling, he made extensive use of modified air bombs. They're highly destructive, and whilst there was evidence he may not have been the first to deploy them in Sarajevo, he was prepared to use them repeatedly on civilians. Major Stevan Veljovic, testifying for the Defence, stated that modified air bombs were "completely inaccurate" and "highly destructive." Transcript 5912, trial judgement 97. This weapon, a 100-, 150-, or 250-kilogramme air bomb designed to be dropped from aircraft had rockets attached to it and was fired from improvised systems fabricated on the back of trucks, trial judgement 95. Often four or five were fired at a time, as Milosevic recognised their inherent inaccuracy, we submit, P701, page 2, paragraph 2, an order of the 21st of April, 1995. He said in an order for an operation due to take place shortly after the 25th of April, 1995: "Proceed forthwith to prepare launchers and make sure that four to six aerial bombs can be launched simultaneously ..." Going back two days he had ordered full combat-readiness for all his troops and to "have launching pads and aerial bombs ready for firing on the town." That's Exhibit D141. Shortly before this, on 6th of April, 1995, Exhibit P226, Milosevic ordered: "The Ilidza Brigade will immediately prepare a launcher with an aerial bomb and transport the bomb for launching. The most profitable target must be selected in Hrasnica or Sokolovic colony," both, we say, Muslim civilian areas, and he continued, "where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted. Inform me personally of readiness for implementation of this task." The weapon that was fired was a 250-kilogramme air bomb. The result of that order, the incident in Hrasnica on the 7th of April, 1995, is recorded in the judgement at 475 to 495, and summarised in this way. Ziba Subo was in her house in Hrasnica with her sons and grandson. She called her sister Ziba Custovic, who lived a few metres away, to come over for coffee. Ziba Custovic never arrived. As she crossed the street, a 250-kilogramme modified air bomb landed in the street killing her. At that moment Ziba Subo described the house "caving in and falling apart." Bricks and plaster fell all over her covering her in rubble, P280, trial judgement 478. She crawled out of the rubble and saw her sister, half her head was missing, she fainted. The Trial Chamber found the bomb destroyed two houses and damaged ten others. Ziba Subo still has back pain and arm pain, her hearing is impaired, as is the hearing of one of her sons who was in the house when the bomb landed. The effect of this instant shelling and sniping was that nowhere was safe, not at home, not in the open, no minute of any day, it was safer during the lulls but even then the population did not feel safe as it never knew when it would start again, trial judgement 743. As one witness described it, life was "like a vacuum, where life was just empty." Trial judgement 746. As Dr. Nakas, the director of one of the hospitals, described it like this: "Each day's work meant exposing yourself to the risk of being added to the long list of the killed and wounded," trial judgement 165, transcript 1062 to 3. Referring to the effects on the population of this endless cycle of killing, Ismet Hadzic said this: "In 1994 and 1995 it became the normal thing, although to say it was normal is horrific. Only the families who had their family members killed were affected. As for the others, they just saw one person less. That was the mental state of the population." Trial judgement 745, transcript 3234. The sniping was so bad that by early July 1995, UNPROFOR reported that almost all civilians had stopped using Zmaja Od Bosne, the main east-to-west thoroughfare in the city and that the snipers who worked that area appeared to have been relocated, trial judgement 226. As one witness put it, trial judgement 745, "they could have coped" with the sniping and shelling of their neighbourhood "until the air bomb landed on the 23rd of July, 1995." Despite this terror, terror that Dragomir Milosevic intended, despite the emptiness in people's lives, the constant fear about their own safety and the safety of their children, despite the countless victims of the actual shelling and sniping, let alone the fear engendered in the entire population, running into tens of thousands of people, despite Dragomir Milosevic's explicit order to shell Hrasnica and cause the greatest casualties, despite the targeting of market-places, food and water queues, the shooting of women and children, the Trial Chamber inexplicably found that mitigating features existed. They credited him as "a man of high moral values," an "altruist," a man who appeared "somewhat troubled by what he was doing." In our submission, it is plain that Dragomir Milosevic could never merit accreditation as "an altruist" or a "man of high moral values." To credit him with altruism or with being a man of high moral values as a mitigating factor in the face of his calculated disregard for the welfare of the thousands of civilians in Sarajevo and the -- and indeed the planned campaign of misery and terror is plainly an error. Altruism, defined in Webster's dictionary as "uncalculated consideration of, regard for, or devotion to others' interests sometimes in accordance with an ethical principle," would appear to be wholly misplaced as a descriptor for Dragomir Milosevic. Likewise, we submit the Trial Chamber was clearly wrong to give him credit for appearing to be "somewhat troubled by what he was doing." It is unclear whether the Trial Chamber accepted he was troubled or that it accepted someone suggested he was troubled. But in any event, the context of the statement in transcript 1783 shows that the reference to being troubled was because his actions may have a consequence for him; that is, that he would not see his daughter again, who (redacted) He was clearly not troubled for the suffering of his victims. Indeed his intent to terrorise the population of an entire city through sniping, using mortars and such indiscriminate weapons as air bombs, together with his explicit order to use such weapons to cause maximum casualties, demonstrates that such a positive finding could not have been established on a balance of probabilities. Further, to credit him with any mitigation for his role in negotiating an anti-sniping agreement, which itself was only necessary because of his continuation of these unlawful acts ignores the entire purpose of the findings relating to the campaign of sniping. In any event, within days of the agreement, Exhibit P6, an UNPROFOR report, records Serb snipers wounding civilians on both the 22nd and 30th of August, 1994, the first incident being one week after the signing. Given the control of snipers was retained at the highest operational level, no credit should have been given for this negotiation. As for orders not to shoot civilians, whilst this may have occurred from time to time, this can have no bearing on his conviction for the crime of terror, indeed the on/off nature of the activity itself added to the fear felt by the victims as acknowledged by the Trial Chamber, trial judgement 743 and 744. Your Honours, in the context of a campaign of terror for over 14 months ordered by Dragomir Milosevic in violation of the Geneva Conventions, it is incomprehensible that any credit could be given to Dragomir Milosevic for his occasional orders to his troops to comply with the Geneva Conventions. The entire strategy being pursued was in direct contravention of those conventions. Every crime was a deliberate contravention. And finally, the voluntary surrender of the accused is itself such an insignificant feature given the magnitude of his crimes, no weight should have been given to it and of itself cannot have resulted in any mitigation in sentence. Your Honours, the sentence of 33 years' imprisonment does not adequately address the magnitude of Dragomir Milosevic's criminal conduct. In Gacumbitsi, the ICTR Appeals Chamber increased a sentence of 30 years' imprisonment to life for an accused of the same age as Dragomir Milosevic. It said: "In light of the massive nature of the crimes and the appellant's leading role in them, as well as the relative insignificance of the mitigating factors, the Trial Chamber ventured outside the scope of its discretion by imposing a sentence of only 30 years ..." Your Honours, this is what we submit happened here. As Your Honours I'm sure will recall, in Galic, in the appeal's judgement, Judge Shahabuddeen, referring to Gacumbitsi said that he believed there was no basis for distinguishing the approach in Gacumbitsi simply because it was a case dealing with genocide. We respectfully adopt that submission. As he further noted in Galic, Galic, like Gacumbitsi, had been convicted of extremely serious offences and Galic lacked any "especially mitigating circumstances." We submit the parallels with Galic in this case are only too obvious, with the distinction that unlike Galic, Milosevic made extensive and repeated use of the air bomb in targeting civilians, to add to the shelling and sniping already established by Galic himself. In our submission, as Judge Shahabud deen observed in Galic in his opinion at paragraph 37, in reviewing the sentence the approach, respectfully, should be this. He said: "The question is not how the sentence imposed appears in absolute terms; thus viewed a sentence of ..." in this case 33 years' imprisonment "... may appear substantial. The question is how the sentence imposed appears in relation to the sentence which is reasonably judged to be merited by the gravity of the appellant's crimes." There is a qualitative difference between 33 years and life, and as the Appeals Chamber has implicitly recognised in Stakic even between 40 years and life. In our submission, Milosevic's crimes were "characterised by exceptional brutality and cruelty, his participation was systematic, prolonged and premeditated and he abused his senior position" of SRK Corps commander. Those were the words used by this Chamber to describe the conduct of General Galic in Your Honours' judgement at paragraph 455. There is nothing to distinguish between Galic and Milosevic sufficient to warrant the imposition of a sentence anything less than life. Indeed, for this case, the case of Galic provides the very comparator that His Honour Judge Meron said was lacking in his dissenting opinion in Galic. Respecting the dissenting opinions in that case, the majority of Judges in the Appeals Chamber considered that these crimes warranted the imposition of a life sentence. In any event, the magnitude of these crimes, their cruelty and their brutality, the effect on the entire population of Sarajevo for 14 months, Milosevic's leading role, his abuse of a high position of authority demonstrate that a life sentence is warranted. Given that this sentence is significantly more serious than a sentence marked in terms of years, even 33 years, the Trial Chamber demonstrably erred in imposing such a sentence. We ask Your Honours to allow the appeal to quash the sentence and impose a sentence of life imprisonment. Your Honours, those are my submissions unless I can assist you or your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. So, please, you can proceed with your submissions, with your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I wish to address a matter that is very important. As a lawyer in criminal law, I had never come upon a case where before someone's guilt was established I would be dealing with mitigating circumstances. At any rate, there is not a single act that a human being may commit which would not be subject to judgement or assessment, especially in a case such as this one involving horrific events transpiring in the former Yugoslavia. In most of these cases the circumstances indeed amounted to a war conflict. It has always been sensitive matters when officers are brought before a Court who have themselves personally not done anything unlawful. I will try to deal with the matter at hand for the short period of time remaining. The branch of law I was dealing with, criminal law, in Yugoslavia, at a time when it was still a fortunate country, the issue of mitigating circumstances was always a very important one. I simply cannot understand how it is possible for someone practicing in criminal law to say that something had been adjudicated in one way in a different case and that this should be applied to the matter at hand. There are no two identical cases in criminal law, there have never been two identical cases. This may be in the interests of the Prosecution to secure another life imprisonment; however, I should like to avoid any comparisons between this case and the Galic case. At the time of trials, archives were opened and documents are available which indicate that there were two warring parties in all these events alleged in the indictment. One mitigating factor could be on the issue of alibi to mention that the accused was wounded when a tank shell was fired from the Zuc hill from a distance of 2 to 3 kilometres, impacting an observation post and hitting Dragomir Milosevic in the head. He survived the impact but lost one eye. This serves to indicate the circumstances in which he had to work. He was in a trench at the time of combat activities, and it goes to show something that I've been discussing the whole day, i.e., the circumstances prevailing in that period. The Trial Chamber showed that the offensive activities conducted throughout that time by the BH army, in particular between May and the end of the war, definitely end until August, the Trial Chamber concluded that these activities were not decisive in arriving at its findings on this issue. However, it is not possible not to proceed from the fact that these combat activities - and I do have sympathy for all those involved, all of us who hail from the area do feel for the individuals who experienced those times -- still, I cannot see how it can have any significance -- how it cannot have significance. The fact that thousands of civilians were killed on the Serb side. We led evidence to that effect. This was a conflict. War engenders fear on both sides. One needs to bear in mind that these events necessarily instilled fear on both sides. I did not called a single officer. Had I managed to call 40 to 50 officers here who, together with Dragomir Milosevic, spent the entire war in trenches, in their own yards, in their own front yards outside their homes, there is not one among them who has not lost a brother or a father. Going back to what the Prosecutor said a moment ago, a shell was fired because the order stated that fire should be opened on civilians. Well, nowhere was it written that civilians should be targeted. When witnesses were testifying about civilians getting killed, there was mention of the fact that the media kept reporting that civilians are targeted. The orders themselves stated that fire should be opened on personnel. I spoke of these orders repeatedly today. Let's look at order 417, page 4 of the English version. Each of the columns contain orders by General Prevljak to act or fire upon forces or personnel, upon men. This is the usual army jargon, and if you look at each of these orders you will see that what is mentioned there is men or forces and not civilians. There is nothing else that I can add on the issue of combat activities. Let me state that 40.000 Serbs lived in that town, and these were brothers and sisters and relatives of the people who were on the other side of the front line. Do you think that this sort of activity could have been employed on Sarajevo when people had their relatives living there? I'm referring to document 415. There was fear present. There was the massacre in Kazani, et cetera. There were such cases spreading fear, but there is absolutely nothing that could be construed in order to interpret the conduct of an individual and to base a sentence on that. Galic was imposed a sentence of 20 years of imprisonment. One of the Judges in that case wanted a ten-year sentence of imprisonment for him. It is my position that you need to take these circumstances into consideration. Does a 70-year-old man need a life imprisonment and can he be imposed life imprisonment in view of these circumstances? To draw such parallels and to formulate such briefs where it is stated that the Trial Chamber established that the crime was committed -- well, these are all individual circumstances. We can't have circumstances across the board. For a man of his age who has spent this much time in detention -- well, I know that you will be considering all these factors before you. Nermin Divovic, a boy of some 10 years of age met his end indeed in a tragic way. I was, in my time, dealing with a great number of serious crimes, and I know that when it comes to acts qualified as murder there are certain allegations in the indictment that would not have even passed the test of the investigation stage. When it comes to Nermin Divovic, the boy who tragically died in the way the Prosecution described, the autopsy report compellingly shows and indisputably shows - and this was also shown by expert witnesses and even though they were expert witnesses of the Defence this does not lessen their expertise - the autopsy report, and it's the only autopsy report of that sort which exists in the evidence, the autopsy report shows that there were two trajectories, one passing through the body of the mother, who survived, and this trajectory was completely in parallel with the ground; the other trajectory passed behind the boy's head and went downward toward the ground. Throughout the war stories were manufactured of how children were being killed in the ABiH-controlled part of Sarajevo. I did refer to that earlier on when I talked about the victims in the BH-held Sarajevo. It will be up to you to evaluate the evidence, but let me refer to the fact that two bullets in this case arrived from the BH army territory, from the side which is opposite to where this notorious Metalka building is located. However, this incident had to be widely reported and it had to be reported in the following day in the newspapers that the Serbs had managed to kill a child with one bullet. That's one matter. The other matter is how Your Honours will be deliberating on the Markale incident. Even Rupert Smith himself said that it is not far-fetched to entertain the idea that it might have been Bosniaks attacking Bosniaks. Nicolai, including others, testified that these were not rumours but that this was the talk of Sarajevo itself, that the Bosniak forces, the forces stationed in Sarajevo, were prone to utilising their own people for political and military purposes. And then if we look at all the victims who were allegedly found in that place - I wouldn't want to go back to the analysis that has to do with that - but one can definitely speak about it in a dramatic and affecting way that the Prosecutor refers to it -- anyway, all the matters that have to do with Markale, please look at the two photographs that I indicated and you will see that those two photographs cannot be linked with the place where the incident occurred. It was not possible to find a person in that place who was killed by buckshot from a hunting rifle or a man who had been shot by a bullet in some other location. When you look at it in that way I think that some things should not be left out of your review in some way, and I'm hoping that you will re-evaluate all of these things, and then I hope that what I have said is sufficient and that when you are making your finding on the sentence, I think that all that has to do with the events that we referred to and that the evidence that has to do with will go in support of everything that I said at the beginning, and that is that you would first need to establish whether this was found to be a civilian zone beyond all reasonable doubt and then only after that would you need to approach the evaluation of all the other matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's nothing that I would wish to add. It's the submissions that I've already made, so I waive the right to reply to any other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Now we come to the end of the submissions of the parties. According to the Scheduling Order now I will turn to Mr. Milosevic, if he wants to address briefly personally the Appeals Chamber for no more than ten minutes he's allowed to do that. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you for this opportunity to address you. I'm going to speak a few words. I accept -- I expect them to be understood only in the way that I meant them to be understood. I would like to say something about the true seal of events on the Sarajevo front. I'm happy that it is no longer a front, that it is a front that is in the past. Very briefly I would like to say something about my life. I came to Sarajevo when I was 14 years old, where I continued my schooling. I had considerable support from my uncle who lived in Sarajevo. I continued my education in Belgrade and then again in Sarajevo. After that, my whole work and life were connected to Bosnia and Herzegovina and primarily Sarajevo. I fell in love in Sarajevo for the first time. I formed my family and I raised and educated my children. Sarajevo became my town and the town of my family. It's a place where I had my family, relatives, friends, colleagues, associates, my best man, and neighbours. In Sarajevo I contributed the taxes and the tax for the construction of Sarajevo, just like any other regular citizen of Sarajevo paid his dues. I cooperated equally and socialised equally with everyone. I would also like to add - perhaps it's not that important - but I would say that my whole property was seized and taken from me in Sarajevo, my property and the property of my family. Sarajevo is an integral part of who I am, a part of my personality. I expected that the search for truth and justice would have greater priority before this Tribunal. The trial proceeded at a considerable pace and it was as if a record was being sought to complete the trial. I didn't have enough time for contacts with my lawyers. I was even denied to send notes in order to direct my lawyers in the courtroom. It seems that the evidence and the testimony of Defence witnesses did not mean that much. I feel that the procedure was irregular and also the attitudes towards me, at least that's how I experienced it. My colleague combatants and my senior officers spoke in a manner that would indicate that they were victims, but they were not understood correctly. There was the question of why they were brought to testify in the first place. It was essential to open up some of these matters more widely. Everything seemed to be happening in a certain context, Your Honour. There is also the fact that many factors and powerful figures did not wish a peaceful resolution for the Sarajevo region. The government and the military leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina sought solutions exclusively on the battle-field. The cease-fire and the end of hostilities could have happened at any point in time. I was never an obstacle to such a way out. There are indications and confirmation that I had given my all to implement the Dayton Peace Accords. This role of mine was seen properly by the French General Bachelet who knew how to appreciate. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: (redacted) General Bachelet, an honourable man, could see that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the people it was protecting in order to carry out this work had accepted to take their own dead from the ground, to gather them up, and as such move out in order to make the implementation of this agreement possible. The Defence placed all the documents at the disposal of this Trial Chamber, the documents of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on the one hand and the documents of the 1st Corps of the Bosnia and Herzegovina army on the other side. And it can be clearly seen that the 1st Corps and other units of the B&H army, from the 1st of August, 1994, until the end of hostilities in 1995, were planning, conducting, and assaulting along the entire Sarajevo front. At that same time the Sarajevo Romanija Corps did not conduct a single attack. It was just working and fighting to prevent a breakthrough by the other side or the advances by the other side. Your Honours, I, as a Corps commander, know best the danger that we were in. Officially I would like to state that it was even worse for us than had we been in hell. At the turbulent Sarajevo front and in the heat of attacks of the forces of the 1st Corps, the MUP forces, the HVO forces, and other components of the B&H army, it was not possible to know if there would be advances from the north-west encircling Vogosca, Ilijas, Rajlovac, Ilidza, and Hadzici, or whether the forces of the 12th Division of the land army and the MUP, there would be an advance out of Sarajevo to cut the roads, surround Grbavica, or whether the forces of the 14th Division of the land army from Igman would set off for Ilidza, Igman, or would they be directed towards Trnovo. All of these areas were defended by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. The commander of the 12th Division of the land army of the B&H army, on the 1st of March, 1995, decided with their brigades to leave Sarajevo to carry out attacks along selected axes. The main reason cited by him - and this has to be cited in the decisions - is to assist, provide help to the 5th Corps in Bihac and this is why this was done. I am asking myself -- this document, D418, I'm asking who was threatening who in this case and was any attention paid to the fact that when somebody launches an attack without any reason, are they doing that because they're under threat or because they are acting on their own whim. This document was admitted. Commanders of the Bosnia and Herzegovina army at all levels made decisions in their combat orders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have to draw your attention to the clock. Your ten minutes have expired. Can you conclude in one minute, please. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to ask you to be allowed to finish. I think I'm almost at the end, but if possible I don't want to finish without completing what I wish to say and what you have given me the opportunity to say. I kindly request to be allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Provided you remain within the time you have -- THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] -- they brought -- yes. The advances were based on decisions to cut certain axes, surround certain sectors, concentric fire, sniper fire, destroy, and come out of the lines, join the other forces, and so on -- well, there's nothing illegal about that. This is something that assault forces do, but it's logical for the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, then, in that case to defend itself. What I am saying I am saying on the basis of documents where this is stated. The B&H army in the Sarajevo front, primarily the 1st Corps, had a force of equivalent of 33 brigades, hill brigades, manoeuvring brigades, motorised brigades, Muslim brigades, guards brigades, special brigades, HVO detachments, and Mujahedin detachments. These units were named glorious units and chivalrous units, and they were all to be faced by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, who had to defend an area of 8.240 kilometres with its eight brigades, the Sarajevo front. They wanted to have a resolution by force. They wanted to bring a resolution by force, by using their pretty powerful forces. Statements, documents, books that were written, as well as assault actions, affirmed the option [as interpreted] that the Bosnia and Herzegovina army had elected General Rasim Delic the commander of that army, stated: "Muslims will continue to fight regardless of peace initiatives. The American peace initiative has no head or tail." This statement was given on the 28th of August, 1995, in Jablanica. This assault operation was carried out, it was called Tegbir, it was initiated on the 14th of June. Here I'm only noting that its consequence were many casualties on both sides. I did not carry out this action. I had to defend myself or oppose such a force. I know that the Prosecution should not be creating an image of the accused as a monster. I don't know what exactly they wanted to do with this story about the residence of my children. I do not like these messages. It is not tenable either that a protected witness, a highly positioned official of the United Nations proclaims me a drunkard and in written documents openly calls me a bandit. I cannot stand drink, and if he had perhaps mistaken our identities, then we need to see if his testimony is accurate because he qualified me with epithets that cannot really be applied to me, not even close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can you conclude your address, please. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Thank you. It is my deep regret and I condemn the numbers of people who were wounded and killed. I feel this deeply in my soul. I know that no mother gave birth to anyone so that they would get killed. It's sad to kill an animal or to break a tree, never mind to kill a human being. And I express my full readiness to pray on the graves of those who were killed and to pray for the fate of seriously disabled persons. I was deeply unhappy when I saw the suffering of people and even now I feel discomfort and pain in my soul. I've seen much suffering of fighters on the field of battle from the 1st Corps of the Bosnia and Herzegovina army and those from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I know very well what it means for innocent civilians to suffer. These are sorry and sad events. And in such a forceful conflict unfortunately I cannot go without mentioning the military casualties. These are human beings too. If you permit me one more minute to give an example. On the 18th of September, 1994, forces of the Bosnia and Herzegovina army, of the 12th Division of that army, organised a break-through towards the east. In that advance that they executed and the support they provided to those people, they actually killed seven people. I watched those people of theirs and I felt bad for them just like I would feel bad about any person, about the way that they were being treated in a building of -- there were eight soldiers of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps who were killed and that were returned to us only when they -- the bodies had began to decompose. I'm talking about victims in each place and in each set of circumstances. If something -- if this is something that anybody will accept and to take into account, I'm deeply regretful about those victims and believe that that is something that should not have happened. I was not the cause of the demise of those victims, but I'm being held responsible here before this Trial Chamber for what the Prosecution is ascribing to me. On the 1st of May, 1993, in Sarajevo, it was announced who war criminals were. In 1992, the names of war criminals were announced. Besides Kukanjac and Radovan Karadzic, it was also announced that Dragomir Milosevic was also a war criminal too, who, up until that time, did not fire a single bullet with his units. I interpret that as something that was meant to happen. It was supposed to happen and that I am a -- a case where it is impossible to prove adequately what happened and who was supposed to do what. I apologise for taking up so much time, but I felt compelled to state these things, even though they may not be taken into account at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Prosecutor, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to rise again. We need to go into private session briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, we can go to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: There's always something wrong. This concludes, I repeat, the appeals hearing in this case. I wish to express my -- on behalf of the Bench, my gratitude to the parties for their submissions, as well as our thanks to all those cooperated with the organisation of the hearing. Special thanks to the interpreters who made the dialogue between the parties and the Bench possible. The appeal judgement will be rendered in due course. The Appeals Chamber will now rise.
